The store sold more than the truck brought, so it has fewer than at the start." If the regrouping gets in the way, do one subtraction on the Exchange Machine first (it deals its own numbers).
note.watch: On the page for everyone, the two steps are printed as a) and b) with boxes, and the dotted space is for the written work. It has three stories from four kinds: a store that gets a delivery and then sells, a market that sells and then gets a delivery, workers who pack on three days, and a truck that leaves things at two stores. The easier page has two stories with numbers that end in 0 (380 + 270). On the harder page, only the answer box is printed, and the child finds the two steps; there, in a truck story, adding the two amounts first and subtracting once is right, too.

3:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.title: Two-step stories: multiply or divide
3:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.objective: Children solve two-step story problems in which one step multiplies or divides within 100 and the other adds or subtracts.

note.mistake: Children miss the word "each" and add: for "There are 6 baskets. Each basket holds 8 medals. 3 are taken out," they compute 6 + 8 − 3. Others multiply and stop. In the sharing stories, some divide the first number they see before they have asked what is being shared.
note.words: On the Baking Tray, set 4 rows of 6 buns: "The baker made 4 rows with 6 buns in each row. How many buns? Which fact?" Write 4 × 6 = 24. "She sells 5." The tray cannot take buns away, so write it: "What happens to the 24?" 24 − 5 = 19. Then tell a sharing story without the tray: "There are 12 pens in a red box and 8 in a blue box. 4 children share all of them fairly. What is being shared? All the pens. What first?" Write 12 + 8 = 20, then 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
note.watch: On the page for everyone, the steps are printed as a) and b): one story multiplies first, one divides first, and one adds the things in two boxes first and then shares. The easier page has two stories that multiply first, with factors from 2 to 5. On the harder page, only the answer box is printed; one story may be "keeps some and shares the rest," where subtracting comes first. A child who cannot say what each number counts (baskets, things in one basket, things taken out) draws the story in the dotted space first.

3:two-step-word-problems#an-equation-wit.title: A letter for the unknown and an estimate to check the answer
3:two-step-word-problems#an-equation-wit.objective: Children write one equation with a letter for the unknown for a two-step story problem, solve it, and check the answer against an estimate from rounded numbers.

note.mistake: Children treat the estimate as one more exercise and never compare it with the answer. Many round the exact answer after they have computed it, which checks nothing. Some think n is the same number in every story; it is only a name for the number we do not know yet.
note.words: Write the store story as one line: 356 + 124 − 213 = n. "n is the number of pencils the store has at the end." Estimate before computing. On the Rounding Hill, choose the ground between two hundreds, shift the hill to 300 and 400, move the boulder to 360 (the spot nearest 356), and let go: it settles into 400. "356 rounds to 400, 124 to 100, 213 to 200. 400 + 100 − 200 = 300." Compute n = 267: "Is 267 near 300? Yes." Then write n = 693: "A child got this. Near 300? No. What went wrong?" (The 213 was added.)
note.watch: On the easier page, the equation is printed and the estimate has a frame of boxes for the rounded numbers. On the page for everyone, the child writes both on lines. The harder page has three stories; the last one prints a child's finished answer, which is right on some pages and far off on others: the child estimates, marks yes or no, and then finds n. No number on these pages ends in 45 to 55, so no one has to argue about a halfway number. A right answer is never more than 100 from the estimate, and a wrong printed answer is at least 200 away: "near" means within about 100.

3:area-model#area-of-a-rectangle-multipl.title: Area of a rectangle: multiply the side lengths
3:area-model#area-of-a-rectangle-multipl.objective: Children find the area of a rectangle by multiplying its two side lengths and say the area with its square unit (24 square feet).

note.mistake: Children add the two side lengths, or add all four sides (they find the perimeter). Others multiply correctly and say the unit of length: "24 feet" for 24 square feet.
note.words: On the Baking Tray, set 4 rows of 6 buns: "How many buns? We don't have to count them one by one: 4 rows of 6 is 4 × 6." Give the tray a quarter turn: "6 rows of 4. Still 24." Draw a rectangle on the board and write 6 ft on top and 4 ft on the left side: "This time no squares are drawn. Picture squares 1 foot on each side. How many fit along the top? How many rows?" Write 4 × 6 = 24 and say the unit: "24 square feet. A square foot is a square that is 1 foot long and 1 foot wide."
note.watch: On the easier page, the squares are still drawn in each rectangle, so a child can check the product by counting. On the page for everyone, only the two side lengths are written. Either order of the two factors is right (6 × 4 or 4 × 6). On the harder page, the sides go from 4 to 10, and two cards show a question mark on one side and print the area ("Area = 54 square meters"): the child finds the side. A child who multiplies 9 × 54 has not read the equation: ask, "What number times 9 makes 54?" The unit changes from card to card, and the area unit is printed with the boxes: have children read it aloud with their answer.

3:area-model#area-of-an-l-shape.title: Area of an L-shape
3:area-model#area-of-an-l-shape.objective: Children cut an L-shaped figure into two rectangles, find the area of each by multiplying, and add the two areas.

note.mistake: Children multiply the two longest sides, as if the figure were a full rectangle. On the page without a grid, they use a side length of the whole figure for one of the parts (for example, 10 where the part is only 6 wide).
note.words: On the Baking Tray, set 5 rows of 6 buns and crack the tray after the third row: "Two trays: 3 rows of 6 and 2 rows of 6. 18 + 12 = 30. Nothing was lost." The tray cannot make an L-shape, so go to the board and draw one on a grid: "This is not one rectangle. It is two rectangles pushed together. Where can one straight cut make two rectangles?" Draw the cut, name the parts A and B, write a product for each, and add. Cut the same figure the other way and add again: "The same area. Either cut is right."
note.watch: On the easier page, the cut is drawn and the parts are named A and B. On the page for everyone, the figure is on a grid without the cut: the child draws the cut, and either of the two cuts is right. On the harder page, there is no grid and the six side lengths are written at the sides. Every length the child needs is printed, for either cut; nothing has to be subtracted. Have the child trace each part with a finger and say its two sides before writing a product. A child who takes the missing corner away from the full rectangle is right; ask for a cut as well, because the boxes add.

3:perimeter#find-the-missing-side.title: Perimeter: find the missing side
3:perimeter#find-the-missing-side.objective: Children find one unknown side length of a figure from its perimeter and the other side lengths, and write an equation with a letter for the unknown side.

note.mistake: Children add the side lengths they see and write that sum as the answer, or they add the perimeter to it. In the rectangle with one side length given, they subtract that side once instead of twice, or they subtract it twice and write what is left as n without halving it.
note.words: On All the Way Round, let the strand lie down: "The distance all the way around is one length." The tool shows no sides and no numbers, so go to the board. Draw a triangle with sides 10 ft and 6 ft and one side n: "The perimeter is 24 feet. Picture its strand laid straight: 24 feet long." Draw the strand as a bar cut into three pieces: 10, 6, n. Write 10 + 6 + n = 24. "10 + 6 is 16. What do we add to 16 to make 24?" n = 8. Check by adding all three sides.
note.watch: On the easier page, the equation is printed under each figure and the child finds n. On the page for everyone, the child writes the equation on the line. The page has triangles, four-sided figures, and five-sided figures. On the harder page, the perimeters go up to 100, one figure is an L-shape with six sides, and two rectangles show one side length and the letter n on two sides. The printed side counts twice; what is left is n + n, so the child still has to split it in two (one side 9, perimeter 30: 9 + 9 + n + n = 30; 12 is left; n = 6). The figures are drawn in proportion (not actual size), so a child can see whether an answer looks right.

2:add-with-blocks#add-two-two-digit-numb.title: Add two two-digit numbers and make a new ten
2:add-with-blocks#add-two-two-digit-numb.objective: Children add two two-digit numbers when the ones make a new ten (36 + 28), with a drawing of sticks and dots on a tens-and-ones mat, and tell why the new ten joins the tens.

note.mistake: Children add each column and write both totals side by side, so 36 + 28 becomes 514 (5 tens, 14 ones). Others circle ten dots and forget to draw the new stick, or draw it and still count the circled dots as ones.
note.words: On the Place Value Lab, build 36 with "Add a ten" and "Add a one." Then add 28 more: two tens and eight ones. "How many ones now? 14. Can we write 14 in the ones place?" The lab asks, "Ten ones! Can you make a ten?" Tap "Make a ten!" and say: "Ten ones make one ten. It joins the tens: 6 tens and 4 ones, 64." Do the same problem on the board with sticks and dots, the dots in rows of five: circle ten dots, draw one new stick, and ask a child to tell why you drew it.
note.watch: On the easier page, both numbers are drawn on the mat, the second under the first (in green); the child circles ten dots, draws the new stick, and counts. On the page for everyone, the mat is empty: the child draws both numbers first, and every problem makes a new ten. On the harder page, two of the six problems make no new ten, so the child has to look before circling. In the boxes under the mat, ten circled dots count as one ten: 6 tens and 4 ones, not 5 tens and 14 ones. When the ones make exactly ten (41 + 29), the child writes 7 tens and 0 ones; watch for an empty ones box.

2:subtract-with-blocks#subtract-and-open.title: Subtract and open a ten
2:subtract-with-blocks#subtract-and-open.objective: Children subtract within 100 when there are not enough ones (52 − 27) by regrouping: they open one ten into ten ones in a drawing of sticks and dots.

note.mistake: Children subtract the smaller ones digit from the larger, no matter which number it is in, so 52 − 27 becomes 35. Others draw the ten dots but do not cross out the stick they opened, so they take 2 tens from 5, not from 4. Some open a ten in every problem, even when there are enough ones.
note.words: The Exchange Machine opens with 48 − 23. "Start at the ones. Are there enough to take 3 away? Yes." Tap "Another sum": 42 − 17. "Enough ones to take 7 away? No, there are only 2." Tap the tens column: one ten crosses over and comes apart into ten ones, and the 4 is crossed out. "We regrouped: 3 tens and 12 ones. It is still 42." Draw the same on the board: four sticks and two dots. Cross out one stick, draw ten dots for it, then cross out 7 dots and 1 stick. "What is left? 2 tens and 5 ones: 25."
note.watch: The easier page takes away a one-digit number; the page for everyone, a two-digit number. On the harder page, the mat is empty and the child draws the first number. Every page has problems that need no ten opened (two on the first two pages, one on the harder page): there the child marks "yes" and only crosses out. Check the yes/no mark first; a wrong mark explains a wrong answer. A first number with no ones (50 − 4) always needs a ten opened; watch for 54. Have children say what the mat shows after the trade ("4 tens and 10 ones") before they cross anything out.

2:column-method#add-three-and-four-two-d.title: Add three and four two-digit numbers
2:column-method#add-three-and-four-two-d.objective: Children add three or four two-digit numbers with a sum within 100 in columns, look for ones that make ten, and write the new tens above the tens column.

note.mistake: Children add the ones, get 18 or 23, and write both digits under the line, so the answer has three digits. Others write the new ten above the tens and forget to add it. When the ones add up to 20 or more, they still write 1 in the small box.
note.words: On the Exchange Machine, tap "Another sum" five times, until 38 + 25 appears. Fill the outlines in the ones column: "8 and 5 make 13. Only one digit fits under the line." Tap the ones column: ten gather into one new ten on the left. The machine adds two numbers only, so go to the board. Write 18 + 36 + 24 in columns. "Look at the ones: 8, 6, 4. Do two of them make ten? 6 and 4. Ten and 8 more is 18." Write 8 under the ones and a small 1 above the tens. "Now the tens: 1 new ten, and 1, 3, 2. That makes 7 tens." 78.
note.watch: On the easier page, there are six problems with three numbers; the ones make no new ten and there is no small box. On the page for everyone, four problems have three numbers and four have four; in each, two of the ones digits make ten, and one new ten goes in the small box. On the harder page, every problem has four numbers and the ones make one or two new tens (8 + 9 + 6 + 0 = 23: write 3 under the ones and 2 in the small box). When the ones make exactly 20, a 0 goes under the ones. Ask children to say the sum of the ones before they write. Have them check by adding from the bottom up.

3:times-tables#multiply-by-tens.title: Multiply by multiples of 10
3:times-tables#multiply-by-tens.objective: Children multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 from 20 to 90 (4 × 60) by thinking in tens: 4 × 6 tens = 24 tens = 240.

note.mistake: Children multiply the digits and leave out the zero, so 4 × 60 becomes 24. Others "add a zero" as a trick and cannot say why, and then write 2,400 or 204. In 5 × 40, some write 20: the fact itself ends in zero (5 × 4 = 20), so they think the zero is already there.
note.words: Draw 4 groups of 6 tens rods on the board, or lay them out. "How many rods are in each group? 6. How many groups? 4. How many rods in all? 4 × 6 = 24. Each rod is a ten, so that is 24 tens. What number is 24 tens?" Ten rods make 100, so 20 tens are 200, and 4 more tens make 240. Write three lines, one under the other: 4 × 6 = 24, 4 × 6 tens = 24 tens, 4 × 60 = 240. "What stays the same in every line? What changes?" Do 5 × 4 tens the same way and ask why the answer has two zeros.
note.watch: Warm up with Times Table of 10; have children read each fact as tens, not "add a zero" (3 × 10 is 3 tens, 30). On the easier page of Multiply by Multiples of 10, six pictures show tens rods in equal groups; the child writes how many tens there are and then the product (2 to 5 groups of 2 to 5 tens). On the page for everyone, each of the eight cards has three lines: the basic fact, the same fact in tens, and the product (3 × 7 = 21, 3 × 7 tens = 21 tens, 3 × 70 = 210). On the harder page, there are twelve equations with no help; in six of them the multiple of 10 comes first (70 × 3). Ask a child who writes 21 for 3 × 70 to say the middle line aloud. Watch the facts that end in zero: 5 × 60 is 30 tens, 300.

3:equivalent-fractions#whole-numbers-as-.title: Whole numbers as fractions
3:equivalent-fractions#whole-numbers-as-.objective: Children write whole numbers as fractions (1 = 4/4, 2 = 8/4, 3 = 3/1) and find the fraction and the whole number at the same point on a number line.

note.mistake: Children think a fraction is always less than 1, so 8/4 looks wrong to them. Others read 4/4 as 4, or write 2 = 2/4 because both numbers are in the problem. Many read 3/1 as one third.
note.words: In Fraction Kitchen, pick Pizza, tap "fourths," and cut. "How many fourths make the whole pizza? 4." Tap "one whole" to check, and write 4/4 = 1. Draw a second pizza in fourths on the board: "Two whole pizzas? 8 fourths: 8/4 = 2." Draw a number line from 0 to 3 and mark it in halves. Count the jumps aloud: "one half, two halves. Two halves land on 1." Write 2/2 under the 1, then 4/2 under the 2 and 6/2 under the 3. "What does the denominator, the bottom number, tell us? How many parts make one whole." Finally, hold up three uncut sheets of paper: "One part makes each whole, so the bottom number is 1. Three parts: 3/1 = 3."
note.watch: On the easier page, one, two, or three whole shapes are shaded completely; the child counts all the shaded parts for the top number (the bottom number is printed) and writes how many wholes that is. Each outlined shape is one whole. On the page for everyone, four number lines are marked in equal parts; the child writes the top number of each fraction under its whole number (the bottom number is printed); the first part (such as 1/3) is labeled. Watch for children who count the marks, not the spaces between them. On the harder page, twelve equations have one number missing (6/6 = _, 3 = _/1, 2 = _/4, _/3 = 2). For 2 = _/4 ask: "How many fourths are in one whole? In two?"

2:arrays#rows-and-columns-of-squares.title: Rows and columns of squares
2:arrays#rows-and-columns-of-squares.objective: Children divide a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares (up to 4 rows and 5 columns) and count the squares by rows.

note.mistake: Children draw the lines freehand, so the squares come out in different sizes, or they draw one line too many. Others mix up rows and columns. When they count, some count the lines they drew, not the squares.
note.words: On The Baking Tray, use the arrow buttons to make 3 rows with 4 in each row. "Rows go across. How many rows? 3. Columns go up and down. How many columns? 4." Count the buns row by row: 4, 8, 12, and write 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Tap "Turn the tray" and ask what changed and what did not (skip the on-screen question about breaking the tray). Now squares instead of buns: give each pair a paper rectangle and square tiles: "Cover it with no gaps or overlaps. How many rows? How many columns?" On the board, draw a rectangle with marks on its sides and show how to lay the ruler from one mark to the mark across from it.
note.watch: Every child needs a ruler. On the easier page, one row and one column of squares are already drawn; the child draws the missing lines and writes the number of rows, columns, and squares. On the page for everyone, there are only marks on all four sides: the child joins each mark to the mark across from it, then adds the squares row by row (4 + 4 + 4 = 12). On the harder page, the marks are on two sides only, so the child must line up the ruler with no second mark to aim at. Each box in the addition gets the number of squares in one row; there are as many boxes as rows. Check the drawing before the numbers: crooked lines make squares of different sizes.

1:measure-length-units#no-gaps-no-overla.title: No gaps, no overlaps
1:measure-length-units#no-gaps-no-overla.objective: Children measure a length by laying paper clips end to end from one end to the other with no gaps and no overlaps, and find the mistakes in rows of clips that were laid wrong.

note.mistake: Children leave gaps between the clips or let them overlap, and still count every clip. Others start the row a little way in from one end of the object, or stop before the other end. Many think any row of clips gives the length, no matter how it is laid.
note.words: On the Measurement Bench (sound on), choose Length and lay paper clips from one end of the object to the other, but leave gaps. Tap "Count." The bench pushes the clips together and says aloud that part of the object is not covered yet. "Why does it need more clips?" Add clips and count again. Then lay a pencil under the document camera and measure it with real paper clips that overlap: "Is my pencil 6 clips long?" Agree on the rule and write it on the board: start at one end, use clips of one size, lay them end to end, no gaps, no overlaps, stop at the other end. Then pairs measure three things from their desks and say "about _ paper clips long."
note.watch: On the easier page, four ribbons each have a row of clips: two rows are laid right, one has gaps, and one has overlaps. On the page for everyone, there are six rows, and one wrong row starts late. On the harder page, one wrong row stops short, and the child writes how many clips long the ribbon is only where the clips are laid right. The child fills in the circle next to "right" or "wrong" and circles every mistake: a row with gaps or overlaps has two, and a row that starts late also runs past the other end. Ask: "Is the number too big or too small?" (A row that starts late may show the right number.)

1:measure-length-units#same-length-two-u.title: Same length, two units
1:measure-length-units#same-length-two-u.objective: Children measure the same object twice, with a longer and a shorter unit (paper clips and cubes or craft sticks, then inches and centimeters), and tell why the smaller unit gives the larger number.

note.mistake: Children think the larger number means the longer object, so a ribbon that is 8 cubes long seems longer than the same ribbon measured as 4 paper clips. Others expect the bigger unit to give the bigger number. Some mix the two units in one row.
note.words: On The Unit Handle, one object sits above two tapes of units, each with its own number (a short end piece left over is not counted). "Both tapes measure the same object." Drag the end of the first tile of the top tape to make its unit smaller. "What happened to the number? Did the object change?" The number goes up; the object and the other tape stay the same. Make the unit bigger: the number goes down. "Smaller unit, more of them." Then pairs measure a pencil, a book, and a glue stick with a classroom ruler, in inches and in centimeters, and say which number is larger and why.
note.watch: On every page, two ribbons are measured with paper clips and cubes, and two with paper clips and craft sticks; a stick is as long as two clips. On the easier page, two cubes are as long as one clip; on the page for everyone, three. On the harder page, the second row is not finished: the child counts the clips and figures out the other unit (4 clips, 2 cubes under the first clip: 8 cubes; 6 clips: 3 sticks). The child writes both numbers and fills in the circle next to the unit it took more of: the cube on the cube rows, the clip on the stick rows. Have every child say why: "It took more cubes because a cube is shorter than a paper clip."

2:line-plots#measure-and-make-a-line-plo.title: Measure and make a line plot
2:line-plots#measure-and-make-a-line-plo.objective: Children measure pencils to the nearest inch, record ten lengths in a table, and show them as Xs on a line plot.

note.mistake: Children draw one X for each different length, not one for each pencil, so three 6-inch pencils get only one X. Others stack the Xs unevenly, so a column of three looks taller than a column of four. When they number the line, some skip the lengths nobody measured.
note.words: On the Ruler, set the units to inches and turn off "Show length." Leave the start handle at 0 and drag the end handle; the bar is the object. "Where does it end? Which inch mark is closest?" Read to the nearest inch. Then draw a number line from 2 to 9 on the board. Ten children each measure a used pencil to the nearest inch and say its length; draw each X above its number: "This pencil is 6 inches long. One X above the 6. Another 6: the new X goes on top of the first." Ask: "Which length do we see most often? How can you tell without counting again?"
note.watch: On the easier page, the ten lengths are printed and the line is numbered: the child draws the Xs, one for each pencil, and answers the questions. On the page for everyone, the child also writes the missing numbers under the line; every tick mark gets a number, even where there will be no X. On the harder page, the table and the line are empty: the child measures ten used pencils with a ruler and numbers the line. Nothing printed on the page is to be measured. Have children cross out each length in the table as they draw its X, and count the Xs at the end: ten. For "how much longer," they count the spaces from the shortest to the longest.

3:line-plot-halves#measure-to-the-quarte.title: Measure to the nearest quarter inch
3:line-plot-halves#measure-to-the-quarte.objective: Children measure lengths to the nearest half and quarter inch on a ruler and show the lengths as Xs on a line plot marked in quarters.

note.mistake: Children count the marks from 0, not the spaces, so every length comes out a quarter inch too long. Others read each small mark as a half (2¼ becomes 2½) or write 2 2/4 for 2½. When a pencil does not start at 0, they write the number where it ends.
note.words: On the Ruler, set the units to inches and turn off "Show length." "How many small spaces in one inch? Eight. So a quarter inch, one of four equal parts, is two spaces." Leave the start handle at 0 and drag the end handle two small spaces past the 2. "How long is the bar? Two inches and one quarter of an inch: 2¼." Turn "Show length" on to check: it reads 2 1/4 in. (If it shows eighths, nudge with the arrow keys.) Do 3½ and 1¾ the same way. Then put the end at 3¼, move the start handle to 1, and ask how long the bar is now (2¼). Give each pair a paper strip and a ruler: they measure it to the nearest quarter inch, say how they know, and add an X to a class line plot.
note.watch: On the easier page, six pencils are each lined up with their own ruler, marked in halves; the lengths are whole and half inches; there is no line plot. On the page for everyone, eight pencils lie on rulers marked in quarters (here one space is a quarter, not two); the child writes each length, draws an X for each pencil on the line plot, and answers two questions. On the harder page, the pencils start at the 1 or the 2, and the child counts the inches and quarter inches from where the pencil starts to where it ends (from 1 to 3¼ is 2¼). The rulers are drawn smaller than a real ruler: the child reads the ruler on the page. On the line plot every quarter inch from 1 to 4 has a labeled tick mark; two pencils of the same length make a stack of two Xs.

1:word-problems#two-kinds-together.title: Put-together stories: how many in all?
1:word-problems#two-kinds-together.objective: Children show stories about one thing in two colors (totals from 4 to 10) with counters of two colors, color pictures to match, and write the addition equation.

note.mistake: Children count one color only, or count the second group from 1 and give that number. Some color the whole row, or write how many pictures the row has. Some write the two numbers and leave the total out.
note.words: On the Number Bonds Board, set the parts to "One for each part" and "Written form" to "One number sentence"; keep "Show the counts" on. Put the cloth over the whole first (the board says numbers aloud until it is covered), then set the number to 8 with − and +, and tap a tray until the left part shows 3 and the right part 5. The board reads ? = 3 + 5. Tell the story in the board's colors: "On the shelf there are 3 orange cups and 5 blue cups. How many cups are on the shelf?" Children count all the counters. Lift the cloth: 8. "Nothing came and nothing went away." The board writes 8 = 3 + 5, the page 3 + 5 = 8: both are true. Then pairs show two of your stories with two-color counters.
note.watch: Each story names one thing in two colors, with a colored dot after each color word. Easier page: three stories, totals 4 to 6, a row of eight pictures. Page for everyone: four stories, totals 5 to 10, a row of ten. The child colors each group, leaves the rest white, and writes _ + _ = _ (the dots under the first two boxes show which group goes where). Harder page: three stories, totals 6 to 10, no pictures: the child draws a circle in its color for each thing. Ask: "How do you know you colored the right number of each?"

2:solids-in-real-life#name-the-solid-sha.title: Name the solid shapes
2:solids-in-real-life#name-the-solid-sha.objective: Children name the sphere, the cube, the cylinder and the cone, match each one to an everyday thing of the same shape, and name it again when it is big or small, standing or lying down.

note.mistake: Children name a solid by its size or the way it lies: a can on its side is "a different shape," and a cone on its tip is "not a cone." Many use flat-shape words for solids (a ball is "a circle," a block "a square"), and some call every box a cube.
note.words: Bring a big and a small ball, a number cube, a can and a party hat. Name each one: "This is a sphere. It is round all over." Roll, stack and slide them: the sphere rolls any way, the cube stacks and slides, the cylinder rolls on its side and stands on a flat end, the cone rolls in a circle. Lay the can down and hold the hat point down: "Still a cylinder? Still a cone?" Turning a solid or changing its size does not change its name. Then children find a sphere, a cube, a cylinder and a cone in the classroom and say each name.
note.watch: At the top of every page, the child draws a line from each of four solids to the thing of the same shape. Below, a color code gives each name a color. Easier page: eight solids, upright, in two sizes. Page for everyone: twelve solids in three sizes, some turned (a cylinder lying down, a cone on its side or tip, a tilted cube). Harder page: the things are an orange, a number cube, a drum and an ice-cream cone, and a box and a pyramid among the twelve are none of the four and stay white. The second page matches three solids to things once more (it has no cone). Ask: "How do you know it is a cylinder, even lying down?"

2:compare-lengths#length-story-problems.title: Length story problems
2:compare-lengths#length-story-problems.objective: Children solve story problems within 100 about lengths given in the same unit (inches or feet): they draw a bar model with a ? for the unknown and write a matching equation.

note.mistake: Children add the two numbers of every story, even when a piece is cut off or two lengths are compared. Many put the longest length in a part of the bar instead of on top, so their equation adds what it should subtract. Others answer with a length the story gives.
note.words: On The Planks, drag the ends to make the top plank 16 and the bottom plank 9. "Which is longer? By how much?" Before moving the piece that sticks out, the class says how long it is: 7. Drag the bracket all the way down to take the piece off and lay it at the end of the short plank: 9 and 7 reach exactly as far as 16. Draw it on the board as a bar: 16 on top, 9 and ? below, and write 16 − 9 = ?. Then tell a story with bigger numbers: "The red ribbon is 63 inches long. The blue ribbon is 48 inches long. How much longer is the red ribbon?" Pairs draw the bar with the longest length on top and write an equation.
note.watch: Every page has three stories about a ribbon, tape, a scarf, a garden hose, or a fence, each in one unit, with a bar, an equation frame, and the unit beside the answer box. On the easier page, the lengths are whole tens, and the first story is done. On the page for everyone, the stories join two lengths, cut one off and compare two. On the harder page, the unknown moves: find the longer or shorter length, or the piece cut off. 63 − 48 = 15 and 48 + 15 = 63 are both right. Ask: "Which length goes on top, and why?"

1:info-text-key-details.title: Facts in the text
1:info-text-key-details.objective: Children ask and answer questions about key details in a short informational text and point to the sentence that tells the answer.

note.mistake: Children answer from what they already know about the animal and not from the text: asked where frogs live, a child writes "in trees" because they have seen a tree frog, although the text says near ponds. Others copy the first sentence that shares a word with the question without reading whether it answers.
note.words: Read the text aloud once while children follow with a finger, then have partners read it to each other. Say: "An informational text teaches us true things. Every answer today is in the text. Put your finger on the sentence that tells you." Ask the first question and have every child point before anyone answers. Then turn it around: "What question could YOU ask that this sentence answers? Start with What, Where, or How." The standard asks children to ask questions as well as answer them.
note.watch: Ask a child, "Where does it say that?" If the finger goes to the picture, the child guessed from the drawing; if it goes nowhere, the answer came from memory. On the page with sentence starters, check that the child finished each sentence with words from the text. On the hardest page, have children write the question number at the start of each underline: one whole sentence for each question, not single words here and there. The on-screen activity is a Kindergarten-level warm-up: use it before the page or for children who need support, not as the practice of the lesson.

1:main-topic-key-details.title: The main topic and key details
1:main-topic-key-details.objective: Children name the main topic of an informational text and retell two or three key details that tell about it.

note.mistake: Children name a detail as the topic: "It is about a sticky tongue." Or they name something the text only mentions, because it is the last thing they read. For key details they pick a small fact, such as how many legs, and leave out what each part of the text is about.
note.words: Say: "The main topic is what the WHOLE text is about. One or two words are enough." Test each choice aloud: "Is every part of the text about a sticky tongue? No, only one sentence. Is every part about frogs? Yes." For the details: "A key detail is an important fact the text teaches about the topic. Look at each heading, then find the important fact in the sentences under it." On the hardest page children need three key details, so one part will give two. Have children tell the topic and the details across their fingers before they write: the thumb for the topic, one finger for each detail.
note.watch: Listen for a child who retells the whole text sentence by sentence: ask for the two or three most important things. A child who writes "animals" has gone too wide; ask, "Which animal?" On the hardest page the details are written in the child's own words. A child who copies a sentence has still found a key detail; ask that child to tell it to you without looking at the text. The on-screen activity is a Kindergarten-level warm-up: use it before the page or for children who need support.

1:text-features.title: Text features: titles, headings, bold words, pictures, captions, and a glossary
1:text-features.objective: Children name the text features of an informational text (title, heading, bold word, picture, caption, glossary) and use headings, bold words, a caption, and a glossary to find facts and word meanings.

note.mistake: Children read the text from the first word to the last to answer every question and never use a heading to jump to the right part. Many skip the caption, because it looks like a decoration under the picture, and take the title for a heading.
note.words: Before reading, go on a feature hunt: "Put your finger on the title. On a heading. On a bold word. On the picture. On the caption. On the glossary." Say: "The title tells what the whole text is about. A heading tells what one part is about. A bold word is important, and you can look it up in the glossary. A caption uses words to tell about the picture." Then model one question from the second page: "It asks about food. Which heading will help me? I read only that part."
note.watch: On "Name the Text Features," check the title and heading boxes first: a child who swaps them needs, "The title is for the whole text; a heading is for one part." A child who writes the picture's number in the caption box needs, "The caption is the words next to the picture." On "Use the Text Features," watch where a child's eyes go after reading a question: to a feature, or back to the first line of the text. For the glossary question, check that the child took the meaning from the glossary and did not make one up. On the hardest "Use the Text Features" page, the caption for the second picture has to tell about THAT picture with a fact from the text: "This is a ___." only names the picture and is not yet a caption that teaches.

2:compare-two-animals#two-fact-files-gra.title: Two animal fact files: same and different
2:compare-two-animals#two-fact-files-gra.objective: Children read fact files about two different animals and find which facts are the same and which are different.

note.mistake: Children compare what they see in the pictures instead of the facts in the table: "They are different because this one is bigger." Size is not one of the four facts. Others stop at the first difference and call the animals different in every way, or write a fact about one animal only when asked what is different.
note.words: Read both fact files aloud, one fact at a time, across the two cards: "What group is the first animal in? And the second? Same or different?" Have children put one finger on each card and move down together. Teach two sentence shapes, and change the verb to fit the fact (are, live, eat, have): "Both ___ and ___ live in ___." for same, and "A ___ eats ___, but a ___ eats ___." for different. Say: "A difference needs BOTH animals in the sentence." This page gets children ready for RI.1.9. The standard itself compares two texts on the SAME topic: to teach it fully, read two short texts about one animal and ask, "What does this text tell that the other one does not?"
note.watch: Check the circles first: a child who circles the same word for every fact, all "same" or all "different," has not read across the two cards. In the written part, look for both animals in each sentence about a difference. In Grade 1, accept short answers and invented spelling; what counts is that the fact comes from the fact files and not from what the child already knows about the animal. The on-screen activity compares two stories, not fact files. Tell children they compare stories the same way: one thing at a time, across both.

K:fact-text-key-details.title: Find the Facts
K:fact-text-key-details.objective: Children listen to a short fact text, read along, and, with support, ask and answer questions about its key details, answering with a picture.

note.mistake: Children answer from what they already know and not from the text: asked where an owl sleeps, a child circles the bed "because you sleep in a bed," although the text says in a tree. Others circle the picture they like best, or the first one in the row.
note.words: Read the text aloud twice while children point under each word. Say: "A fact text tells us true things. Today every answer is in the text." Read one question at a time. Then reread the text one sentence at a time and say, "Thumbs up when you hear the answer." Then: "Put your finger on that sentence." Only then do children circle or draw. On the page with two questions to draw, the last box asks for a question of the child's own: give a starter, "Ask me something about owls. Start with What or Where," and write the question down for a child who cannot yet. Then read the text again together: does it answer the question? If not, say, "That is a great question to find out more about."
note.watch: Ask a child, "How do you know?" A child who points to the sentence has used the text; a child who says "I just know" needs the sentence read again. On the drawing pages, a drawing counts when the child can tell you what it is and which sentence it comes from; the drawing does not have to be good. The on-screen activity shows a two-sentence fact, and the child taps its key detail. Children read it on their own, so use it with a small group or sit beside children who cannot yet read it.

K:fact-text-main-topic.title: What Is It All About?
K:fact-text-main-topic.objective: Children say what a whole fact text is about (its main topic) and tell one or two things the text says about it.

note.mistake: Children pick a detail as the topic: for the text about cows they circle the milk, because milk is in two of the four sentences. Asked for a detail, they tell something they know that the text never says.
note.words: Say: "The topic is what the WHOLE text is about." Point to a detail picture in the first row (on the cow page, the milk) and ask, "Is every sentence about this?" Read the sentences one by one and have children show a thumb up or down for each. "Is every sentence about cows? Then cows is the topic." For the details: "Tell me one thing the text says about cows. And one more." Have children say each detail in a whole sentence before they circle or draw it.
note.watch: In the first row, a child who circles a detail picture does not yet see that the topic is what every sentence is about. On the drawing pages, ask the child to tell you the two details and check that both are in the text. On the hardest page, children may copy a word from the text or sound it out; accept invented spelling. The on-screen activity asks what a short text read aloud is all about (its topic): a good warm-up before the page.

K:pictures-and-text.title: Pictures That Teach
K:pictures-and-text.objective: Children match each sentence of a fact text to the picture that goes with it and tell what the picture shows.

note.mistake: Children draw a line to the nearest picture, or match by one word they catch: "leaves" in a sentence about a nest pulls them to the picture of a tree. On the page with a missing picture they draw the animal or thing of the text again, not what the sentence without a picture tells about.
note.words: Read the first sentence aloud and ask, "Which picture shows this? Tell me what you see in it." Say: "Every picture goes with one sentence. If two pictures seem to fit, listen to the other sentences first: each picture is used one time." Have children trace the line with a finger before they draw it. For the empty box: "Which sentence has no picture yet? Draw what THAT sentence tells about."
note.watch: Look for two lines that end at one picture: the child matched by a single word. Read the other sentences to the child again and have the child use each picture once. On the easiest page there are three sentences, on the others four. Ask each child about one line, "What part of this sentence does the picture show you?": the standard is about telling how a picture and the words go together, not only about drawing the line. The on-screen activity reads one part of a story aloud and asks which picture shows it. It uses stories, not fact texts: use it as a warm-up or at a center, and afterward ask, "How did the picture help you?"

K:first-then.title: First, Then
K:first-then.objective: Children tell what comes first and what comes next in a fact text that tells a change.

note.mistake: Children put the two things in the order they like or in the order of the pictures on the strip, not in the order of the text. On the drawing pages they draw the first two things the text names and not the two the question asks about.
note.words: Read the text aloud, then the question in the box: it tells which change the page is about. Say: "What was there FIRST? What did it turn into, or what came NEXT?" Have children answer in one sentence with both words: "First it is a caterpillar, then it is a butterfly." On the cut-and-glue page say: "Three pictures, two boxes. One picture is not part of the answer; it is left over."
note.watch: Before the glue comes out, have each child lay the two pictures in the boxes and tell you the sentence with first and then. A child who reverses them should hear the text once more and listen for the words that tell the change, like "turns into," "grows into," or "then." On the hardest page, children may copy the two words from the text or sound them out; accept invented spelling. The on-screen activity shows one fact and asks which fact comes next or happens because of it: use it after the page, and ask, "How do these two facts go together?"

2:main-topic-paragraphs.title: The Main Topic and Each Paragraph
2:main-topic-paragraphs.objective: Children name the main topic of an informational text of three paragraphs and tell what each paragraph is mostly about.

note.mistake: Children name a detail as the main topic ("how beavers slap their tails") or a topic that is too wide ("animals that live in water"). For a paragraph they copy its first sentence instead of saying what the whole paragraph is mostly about, or they tell something from another paragraph.
note.words: The text is printed as three numbered paragraphs with no title and no headings, so children have to find the topic themselves. Read it once together. Ask: "What is every paragraph about? That is the main topic of the whole text." Then cover two paragraphs with a sheet of paper and reread the third: "What is THIS paragraph mostly about? Say it in a few words." On the easiest page, children read four statements and write the number of the paragraph next to each one. One statement fits no paragraph, so its box stays empty: say so before they start.
note.watch: A child who writes the same number twice has matched by a single word: have the child reread that paragraph and show you the sentences that fit the statement. On the writing pages, accept any wording that fits the whole paragraph; "what beavers build" is as good as the answer on the key. On the hardest page children also write a heading for each paragraph: a good heading is short and fits every sentence under it. In the on-screen activity children read short articles and tap the card that names the main topic, not a small detail: a quick check before or after the page.

2:text-features.title: Text Features: Glossary and Index
2:text-features.objective: Children name the features of an informational text (title, headings, bold words, captions, glossary, index) and use them to find facts quickly.

note.mistake: Children mix up the glossary and the index: both are lists of words at the end of a text. They reread the whole text to answer a question that a heading or the index answers in a moment. Some read the number beside an index word as an amount, not as the place to look.
note.words: Start with the page Name the Text Features. Six lettered dots are placed on six parts of the text, and children write each letter next to the name of the part. Then ask about each part: "What is its job?" Say: "The glossary tells what a word MEANS. The index tells WHERE you can read about it." The three parts of each text are numbered 1, 2, and 3, like the pages of a small book, and the index names these numbers. On the page Glossary and Index, read each question and ask first, "Which part of the text will help us fastest?" Only then do children look for the answer.
note.watch: Ask a child to show you with a finger how the answer was found: a finger that goes straight to the heading, the caption, or the index shows that the feature is being used. On the hardest page children add one word to the index and one to the glossary. The index word has to stand in the text, with the number of its part beside it. The glossary entry has to tell what the word means; the child's own words are fine.

2:diagram-and-text.title: What the Diagram Shows
2:diagram-and-text.objective: Children read a diagram with labels and arrows together with a text, answer questions from the diagram, and tell what the diagram adds to the text.

note.mistake: Children read the diagram like a sentence, from left to right, and stop at the last picture: they do not follow the long arrow back to the first stage. They answer a diagram question from memory or from the text. Asked what the diagram shows that the text does not, they repeat a sentence of the text.
note.words: Say: "A diagram is a picture that explains. The labels name each part, and the arrows show what comes next." Follow every arrow with a finger, including the long one at the bottom: "Where does it lead? Why?" Then compare: "The text tells what happens. Does it tell the NAMES of the stages? Where do we find them?" On the page Text or Diagram?, children check where they learn each fact; have them point to the sentence or to the place in the diagram first. Each fact is learned in one place only. Before reading, explain stage, phase, and, for the moon, quarter (a quarter moon looks like half a circle), but do not pre-teach caterpillar, chrysalis, larva, pupa, froglet, sprout, or seedling: the diagram teaches them.
note.watch: On the hardest page of What the Diagram Shows, one label and one arrow are missing. The name of the stage without a label is in the text; accept other true names too ("bean seed," "adult frog"). The arrow belongs in the gap between two stages and points to the right. For what the diagram shows that the text does not, and for the fact a child writes on Text or Diagram?, accept any true answer the child can point to: a stage name, the order, what a drawing shows. A fact that both tell, such as "butterflies lay eggs," does not count. On the moon page the long arrow also shows that the phases repeat; the text adds how often.

2:steps-in-order.title: Steps in Order: How It Is Made
2:steps-in-order.objective: Children describe the steps of a how-it-is-made text in order with the words first, next, then, and finally, and tell why one step has to come before another.

note.mistake: Children put the best-known step first (the bread in the oven) or keep the order in which the mixed-up steps appear on the page. In their own sentences they begin every step with "then." Asked why a step has to come first, they answer "because the text says so."
note.words: Read the text and have children put a finger on First, Next, Then, and Finally: "Each of these words tells us that a new step starts." Have four children say the four steps aloud in order, one step each, before anyone writes. On the easiest page the four steps are mixed up, and children number them 1 to 4. On the page Before and After, each sentence tells about two steps: "Which of the two happens earlier? Find both in the text." For the why-question ask: "What would go wrong if we left this step out?" Explain these words before reading, because the text uses them: hive, honeycomb, wax, dough, crust, mill, pulp, germs, cartons, grove, grease, yarn.
note.watch: On the writing pages a step is right when it tells what happens, in the child's own words; it does not have to match the key. Each box has two lines, so a whole sentence fits. Look at the first words: a child who writes "First, ... Next, ... Then, ... Finally, ..." has the order words; a child who writes "then" four times needs the four words on the board. A good why-answer names what the earlier step makes or changes: the chips have to be cooked because the sheet is made from pulp. On the page Before and After, a question about "the step right before" or "the step right after" is answered by anything that happens in that step: accept every action its paragraph tells. In the sentences that begin with Before or After, any earlier (or later) step makes a true sentence; the key shows only the nearest one.

2:compare-two-animals.title: Two Animals: Same and Different
2:compare-two-animals.objective: Children compare the facts of two animal fact files, sort them into same and different, and write what they found in sentences that name both animals.

note.mistake: Children write a fact about one animal ("The eagle has feathers.") where the page asks for a comparison. Some decide by what they picture, not by the fact files: "A ladybug is small and an eagle is big," which neither fact file says.
note.words: Before anyone writes, draw a chart with three columns on the board: the fact, the first animal, the second animal. Fill it in together from the two fact files and mark each row S or D. Then turn rows into sentences with the comparing words of Grade 2: both, and, too for what is the same; but, while, unlike for what is different. Model one of each: "Both animals eat meat." "The ladybug is an insect, but the eagle is a bird." The Grade 2 standard asks children to compare the most important points of two texts on the SAME topic. This page compares two animals, so end the lesson with two short texts about one animal and ask, "Which point do both texts make? What does only one of them tell?"
note.watch: Read the four sentences each child wrote. A sentence about a difference has to name both animals and both facts; "They are different" is not enough. A sentence about what is the same should use both or too. If a child circled every row the same way, cover all rows but one and compare just that row. The on-screen activity compares two stories; the steps are the same: one point at a time, across both.

K:two-texts-one-topic.title: Two Texts, One Topic
K:two-texts-one-topic.objective: With help, children tell what two short fact texts on one topic both say and what only one of them says.

note.mistake: Children sort by what they know, not by what the texts say: a cat may play with a ball too, so the ball goes in the middle, although only the text about dogs tells about a ball. Many children wear boots in the snow, but only the rainy-day text tells about boots. Others glue a card under the first text that names it and never check the second text. Most cards can be placed from what children already know, so a correct page does not prove they compared the texts. The proof is pointing to the sentence in each text.
note.words: Read the first text aloud, then the second, while children point under the words. Say: "Both texts are about pets" (or trees, the weather, the sky, farm animals). "Some things are in both texts. Some are in only one." Hold up one picture card and name it with the word of the text ("leaves," "rain boots," "yarn," "a mail truck"): "Listen for it." Read both texts again, and children raise a hand each time they hear the word. "Did you hear it in the first text? In the second? In both?" Only then do they glue the card. The picture of each text is at the top of its box, and the middle box shows both pictures.
note.watch: Ask about one card in the middle: "Show me where each text says it." A child who can point to both sentences has compared the texts. On the cut-and-glue page, two pictures go in each box. On the drawing pages, anything a text tells about counts, and a quick sketch is fine; on the draw-and-write page invented spelling is fine too. A drawing of the cat or the dog only copies the picture at the top: ask for something the text says about it. The on-screen activity compares two stories, not fact texts: use it as a warm-up or at a center, and tell children they do the same thing here with facts.

K:read-picture-book.title: Read a little book
K:read-picture-book.objective: Children read a little book with one repeated sentence pattern, pointing under each word, and tell what the book is about.

note.mistake: Children say the sentence from memory and from the picture without looking at the words: they point three times for four words, or say "lamb" where the book says "sheep." Others stop pointing after the first page.
note.words: Fold the page into a little book together: top half back, then left half back. Name the pictures first, so that every child has the words. Read the title and page 2 aloud, pointing under each word; then children read pages 3 and 4 themselves. Say: "One touch for each word. Does your finger stop when your voice stops?" If a child says a word that fits the picture but not the print, point to the first letter: "Could this be lamb? What letter would lamb start with?" If the word can be sounded out, like pig, have the child say each sound and blend it: /p/ /i/ /g/, pig. Then use the Read and Talk page: read the new words and the picture words together, read the book again, and talk about the three questions.
note.watch: Watch the pointing finger, not just the voice: one touch for each word shows that the child matches spoken words to printed words. A child who reads the pattern on every page but cannot point to a word you name ("Show me the word the.") is reciting: go back to the sight-word lesson. Each book is marked with a level. (A Level A book has one short line on each page and repeats one sentence pattern; only the picture word changes.) Each time children reread the book, they check one box next to "I read it" on the Read and Talk page. A child who reads the book easily is ready for another book of the same level.

3:answer-with-evidence.title: Answer with Evidence
3:answer-with-evidence.objective: Children ask and answer questions about an informational text and show the paragraph and the sentence that prove each answer.

note.mistake: Children answer from what they think they know ("Penguins live at the North Pole") instead of from the text, or they name the paragraph where they first saw a word of the question. Asked to prove an answer, they copy the first sentence of the paragraph. Their own questions ask something the text does not answer ("Do astronauts get scared?").
note.words: Read the text once together; the paragraphs are numbered. Model one question aloud: "How do I know? I put my finger on the sentence that tells me. It is in paragraph 2." Use the sentence frame "The text says ..." on both days. On Level 1 of the Answer with Evidence page the paragraph number is printed after each question; on Level 2 children find the paragraph themselves; on Level 3 they also copy the sentence that proves the answer. On the Ask and Answer page a sentence from the text is the answer, and children find or write the question. Say: "A question word tells what kind of answer is coming: where asks for a place, when for a time, why for a reason, how for a way, who for a person." Before reading, teach the hard words of your text, such as lens, laboratory, huddle, telegraph, or baleen.
note.watch: An answer is right when the text supports it, in the child's own words or in the words of the text; a full sentence is not required. The paragraph number has to match: a child with the right answer and the wrong number probably answered from memory or matched a single word, so have the child go back and touch the sentence. On Level 3, accept any sentence of the right paragraph that proves the answer; the key shows one. For a child's own questions, check three things: the text answers the question, the answer is correct, and the paragraph number is where the answer is found.

3:main-idea-key-details.title: Main Idea and Key Details
3:main-idea-key-details.objective: Children tell what each paragraph of an informational text is mostly about, determine the main idea, and explain how the key details support it.

note.mistake: Children give the topic in one word ("lighthouses") instead of the main idea, which is a whole sentence about the topic. Or they pick the most interesting detail (a blue whale's tongue can weigh as much as an elephant), or a sentence so broad that it could fit a hundred other texts ("Many animals live in the ocean"). For a summary they copy the first sentence of each paragraph.
note.words: Start with the Main Idea of Each Paragraph page: the text is printed without its headings. Cover three paragraphs with a sheet of paper and read one: "What do all these sentences tell about?" Then move to the Main Idea and Key Details page: "The topic is what the text is about: blue whales. The main idea is what the text says about the topic, in a sentence." Test a main idea with the question "Does every paragraph fit under it?" A sentence that only one paragraph fits under is a detail (too narrow); a sentence that could fit many other texts is too broad. Key details hold the main idea up; ask of each: "How does it help show the main idea?" For the summary on Level 3 say: "Main idea first, then two or three key details, in your own words."
note.watch: On the writing levels, accept any main idea that is a sentence, names the topic, and fits all four paragraphs; it does not have to match the key. A child who writes "It is about penguins" has the topic: ask "What does the text say about penguins?" A small fact, such as a single year or number, is usually a detail, not a key detail. On Level 1 of the Main Idea and Key Details page one of the four sentences is not in the text: a child who checks it has not gone back to the text. In a summary, look for the main idea and at least two key details, and no copied sentences.

3:text-features-search-tools.title: Text Features and Search Tools
3:text-features-search-tools.objective: Children use the table of contents, headings, key words in bold, a sidebar, the glossary, and the index of a text to find information quickly.

note.mistake: Children reread the whole text to answer a find-it question instead of going to the text feature that takes them straight there. They mix up the table of contents (the chapters in the order of the book) and the index (important words in ABC order with every page they are on). They skip the sidebar because it sits outside the main text.
note.words: The text is printed as a small book: each paragraph is a page with its page number, and the book has a table of contents, a key word in bold on every page, a sidebar, a glossary, and an index. Point to each text feature and name its job: "The table of contents lists the chapters in order and the page where each begins. The index lists important words in ABC order and every page that tells about them. The glossary tells what the key words in bold mean. A sidebar gives an extra fact." On Levels 1 and 2 of the Use the Text Features page each question names the feature; on Level 3 children write the answer and the letter of the feature that helped them find it. On the Which Text Feature? page they decide which feature they would use. Bring a real nonfiction book and find its table of contents, glossary, and index together.
note.watch: Watch how a child finds an answer, not only the answer: a child who reads every page to find "fog" has not used the index. An index answer has to name every page, not just the first one. For the index task of Level 3, accept any important word that really stands on the named page, with that page number. On Levels 1 and 2 of the Which Text Feature? page one feature is left over, the heading: the table of contents shows all the headings in one place. On Level 3 a child's own question is right when the feature answers it (what a word means for the glossary, which pages tell about a word for the index).

3:events-cause-effect.title: Events in Order, Cause and Effect
3:events-cause-effect.objective: Children describe how the events, steps, and ideas in an informational text connect, using words of time and sequence and of cause and effect (because, so).

note.mistake: Children list facts in the order they remember them, not in the order of the text, and begin every sentence with "then." They turn cause and effect around ("The Pony Express closed, so a telegraph line was built"). With because and so they pick the wrong word: "because" goes before the cause, "so" goes before the effect.
note.words: Say: "A cause makes something happen. The effect is what happens. Ask 'Why did it happen?' to find the cause, and 'What happened because of it?' to find the effect." Model with a pair from the classroom and say it both ways: "It started to rain, so we had recess inside. We had recess inside because it started to rain." On the Events in Order page the task names what the four events or steps tell (for example, how a blue whale breathes); have children find that part of the text first. On Level 3 they also choose one event and tell why it happens or what it leads to. On the Cause and Effect page, Level 1 matches causes with effects; on Level 2 children write the missing half; on Level 3 they also write both halves as one sentence with because or so.
note.watch: On the writing levels an event or an effect is right when it comes from the text, in the child's own words; it does not have to match the key. In a chain, check the order against the text: what comes first in the text, or what causes the next thing, comes first. In the one-sentence task, check the direction: the cause comes after "because" or before "so." A child who writes two sentences without because or so has the facts but not the connection: ask "Which one made the other happen?" If a child matches an effect to the wrong cause, have the child read the pair aloud with "so" between them and ask whether the text says that.

3:story-evidence.title: Show Where the Story Says It
3:story-evidence.objective: Children ask and answer questions about a story and show the paragraph and the sentence that prove each answer.

note.mistake: Children answer from a version of the story they already know instead of from this text. They give the right answer with the wrong paragraph, or copy a sentence that is near the answer but does not prove it. Their own questions ask about things the story does not tell ("What was the lion's name?").
note.words: Read the story aloud once, then have children read it again on their own; the paragraphs are numbered. Model: "How do I know? I put my finger on the sentence. The story says ..." On Level 1 of the Show Where the Story Says It page the paragraph number is printed after each question; on Level 2 children find the paragraph; on Level 3 they also copy the sentence that proves the answer. On the Ask and Answer About a Story page a sentence from the story is the answer, and children circle or write the question; on Level 3 they write three questions of their own. Remind them: who asks for a character, what for a thing or an event, where for a place, when for a time, why for a reason, how for a way. A good question can be answered by pointing to the story.
note.watch: An answer is right when the story supports it; a full sentence is not required. Check the paragraph number: a child with the right answer and the wrong number probably answered from memory, so have the child touch the sentence. On Level 3, accept any sentence that proves the answer; the key shows one. A child's own question is right when it begins with the given word, the story answers it, and the paragraph number is where the answer is found.

3:central-message.title: Retell a Story and Find Its Central Message
3:central-message.objective: Children retell a fable or folktale in order, determine its central message, and explain how the events of the story show it.

note.mistake: Children retell every detail instead of the main events, or they leave out the ending. For the message they retell what happens ("The mouse helps the lion") or give a rule about the characters ("Lions should watch out for hunters") instead of a lesson for people. Some pick a lesson they know from another story.
note.words: Start with the Retell the Story page: "What are the most important events? What can we leave out?" On Level 1 children number four given events; on Levels 2 and 3 they write the four main events after First, Next, Then, Finally. Then turn to the Central Message page: "A fable or folktale teaches a lesson about how people should act. The lesson is not about lions or mice; it is about us." Ask: "What did the character learn? What should we learn?" On Level 1 children choose the message from three sentences and check the three events that show it; on Level 2 they write the message and three events; on Level 3 they also tell how the ending teaches the message.
note.watch: Accept any message that is a lesson for people and fits the whole story; it does not have to match the key. "The mouse saved the lion" is a retelling, not a message: ask "So what does that teach us?" On Level 1 of the Central Message page one of the four sentences is not in the story: a child who checks it has not gone back to the text. In a retelling, look for the problem and the ending, in order; small details may be left out. The events a child lists for the message should show it, not be just any three events.

3:characters-actions.title: Characters: Traits, Feelings, and Actions
3:characters-actions.objective: Children describe the characters of a story by their traits and feelings and explain how what the characters do leads to what happens next.

note.mistake: Children describe how a character looks ("big," "small") instead of what the character is like, or they name a feeling ("happy") when a trait is asked. They give a trait without a sentence that shows it. In cause and effect they turn the two around, or they pair two things that both happen without one making the other happen.
note.words: Say: "A trait is what a character is like inside, not just for a moment: clever, proud, patient. A feeling can change: the fox is pleased at first and sorry at the end. We learn traits from what characters say and do." On Level 1 of the Character Traits page children circle a trait and write the letter of the sentence that shows it; on Level 2 they choose a word from the list and copy the sentence; on Level 3 they find a word of their own and tell how a character feels at the end. On the Cause and Effect in a Story page ask: "What happened? What happened because of it?" Level 1 matches causes with effects; on Level 2 children write the missing half; on Level 3 they also write both as one sentence with because or so.
note.watch: On Level 3 accept any trait word that fits and that the copied sentence shows: "smart" for clever, "impolite" for rude. In The Crow and the Pitcher both words describe the crow; accept them in either order. A word about looks or a passing feeling is not a trait: ask "What is the character like inside, not just for a moment?" In the one-sentence task, check the direction: the cause comes after "because" or before "so." On the writing levels accept any cause or effect that the story tells; the key shows one.

3:story-discussion.title: Talk About a Story
3:story-discussion.objective: Children come to a group talk prepared, having read the story, and use their notes and the story itself to explain their ideas.

note.mistake: Children come to the talk without having marked anything and say only "I liked it." They give an opinion without a reason from the story, or they repeat what the last speaker said. Some read their notes aloud and stop listening to the others.
note.words: Day 1: children read the story and fill in the Get Ready to Talk About a Story page: a part that surprised them with its paragraph, a question for the group, and (Levels 2 and 3) the words they will read aloud. Day 2: groups of four with the same story meet with the Talk About the Story page; give about ten minutes to write an idea for each question first, and start with the questions everyone has. Draw a name stick for the first speaker, who reads a question and gives an idea with its paragraph; each next child adds on, agrees, or disagrees. Practice the sentence starters printed on the page: "I think ... because the story says ...," "I agree with ... because ...," "I see it differently because ...," "Can you show where the story says that?"
note.watch: These pages have no answer key: every answer that the story supports is right. Look at the notes before the talk: a child with an empty page is not prepared, so pair the child with a partner to mark one part. During the talk, listen for the paragraph: a child who says "in paragraph 3 it says ..." is using the story. Listen also for links to what others said ("I agree with Maya because ..."). For a question about what might happen next, any paragraph that gives a reason counts.

2:character-challenge.title: How Characters Meet a Challenge
2:character-challenge.objective: Children describe how a character in a story responds to a problem: what the character does, how the character feels, and what happens because of it.

note.mistake: Children retell the whole story instead of naming the problem. They say what the character should have done, not what the character did, or they give their own feeling ("I would be sad") for the character's. In cause and effect they write two things that happen one after the other without one making the other happen.
note.words: Read the story aloud once, then read it together. Ask three questions in the same order every time: "What happens to the character? What does the character do about it? How does the character feel?" Have children point to the sentence that tells them. On Level 1 of the How a Character Meets a Challenge page children circle answers; on Level 2 they write them; on Level 3 they also tell what they would have done in the character's place. On the What Happens and Why page say: "A cause makes something happen. The effect is what happens." Try each pair aloud with "so" between the two: "The hare felt sure that he would win, so he lay down for a nap." On Level 3 children write one pair as a sentence with because or so.
note.watch: An answer is right when the story supports it, in the child's own words. For the feeling, accept a word that fits the story even if it is not the word on the key: "embarrassed" for ashamed, "scared" for afraid. Ask "How do you know?" and have the child show the sentence. On Level 3, any choice is fine if the reason fits the story. In the one-sentence task, check the direction: the cause comes after "because" or before "so."

2:fable-lesson.title: Fables: What Is the Lesson?
2:fable-lesson.objective: Children retell a fable by its beginning, middle, and end and tell the lesson it teaches.

note.mistake: Children retell only the part they liked best, or they tell the middle and the end and leave out how the story begins. For the lesson they repeat what happens ("The tortoise won") or give a rule about the animals ("Hares should not nap") instead of a lesson for people.
note.words: Tell children: "A fable is a short story that teaches a lesson. Often its characters are animals or things that act like people." Start with the Beginning, Middle, and End page: on Level 1 children put three sentences in order; on Levels 2 and 3 they write the three parts themselves (save Level 3 for Day 2, or model one lesson first: it also asks for the lesson). Hold up three fingers: "First ... then ... in the end ..." Then turn to the What Is the Lesson? page: "What did the character learn? What can we learn from it?" On Level 1 children circle the lesson and check the two sentences that show it; on Level 2 they write the lesson and what a character does that shows it; on Level 3 they also tell how the ending teaches the lesson. Have children say the lesson so that it fits a person, not only a hare or a dog.
note.watch: A retelling is right when the three parts are in order and the ending is there; small details may be left out, and it does not have to match the key. Accept any lesson that is about people and fits the whole story. "The tortoise won the race" is a retelling: ask "So what does the story teach us?" On Level 1 of the What Is the Lesson? page one of the three sentences is not in the story: a child who checks it has not gone back to the story.

1:story-key-details.title: Find the Answer in the Story
1:story-key-details.objective: Children answer questions about key details in a short story and show the sentence that tells the answer.

note.mistake: Children answer from what they already know about the animals ("Owls fly at night"), not from what the story says. Some copy the first sentence that holds a word of the question. On Level 2 they write the missing words but forget the period.
note.words: Read the story aloud once while children follow with a finger, then read it together. Say: "The answer is in the story. Put your finger on the sentence that tells you." Model the first question: read it, find the sentence, read that sentence aloud, then answer. On Level 1 children circle one of three answers. On Level 2 the answer starts on the line and children finish it. On Level 3 they answer three of the questions in a whole sentence and underline the sentence in the story that tells each answer. Children who finish early ask a partner one more question that the story answers: "Who ...?" "Where ...?" "What ...?" On screen, Fable's Picture Stories gives more practice with questions about three-picture stories.
note.watch: An answer is right when the story says it. On Levels 2 and 3 accept the child's own words and any spelling you can read; on Level 3 look for a capital letter at the start, on Levels 2 and 3 for a period at the end. Accept every answer the story supports: "home" or "up the hill" for where Sam wants to take the apple. If a child answers without looking back, ask: "Where does the story say that?" On Level 3 the underlined sentence matters as much as the answer.

1:characters-setting-events.title: Characters, Setting, and Big Events
1:characters-setting-events.objective: Children tell who is in a story, where it takes place, and the big thing that happens, with details from the story.

note.mistake: Children name only one character, or they add an animal that is not in the story. For the setting they tell when ("at night") but not where. For the big event they pick the first thing that happens or a small detail.
note.words: Teach three words with a gesture each: characters (point to a person), setting (spread your arms for the place), event (clap once: something happens). Say: "Characters are who the story is about. The setting is where and when it happens. A big event is an important thing that happens." Read the story, then ask: "Who? Where? What is the big thing that happens?" On Level 1 the story is printed without pictures: children read who is in it and circle the two characters among four animals, then the setting and the big event. On Level 2 they write a word or a few words in each box. On Level 3 they write one sentence in each box; ask for one detail, such as what kind of animal a character is. On screen, Marlo's Magnifier asks for the detail that proves something about a character.
note.watch: On Level 1 exactly two animals are circled. On Levels 2 and 3 accept names or animals ("Ben and Fay" or "a bear and a fox") and any true wording of the place and of the big event. The big event is right when the story would not work without it: Ben sharing his plums, not Fay sitting in the park. Ask: "Could we tell the story without this?" If a child says that owls eat mice, say: "In this story Ola is a friend. In stories, animals can act like people."

1:retell-and-lesson.title: Retell the Story and Tell Its Lesson
1:retell-and-lesson.objective: Children retell a story by its beginning, middle, and end and tell the lesson it teaches.

note.mistake: Children retell only the end, or they tell every sentence instead of the three big parts. For the lesson they say what happened ("Ben gave Fay plums") instead of what we can learn from it.
note.words: Hold up three fingers: "First ... Then ... In the end ..." Retell a story the class knows in three sentences before children try. On Level 1 children put three sentences in order and circle the lesson. On Level 2 they write one sentence for the beginning, the middle, and the end with the help of a word bank, then circle the lesson.
