On Level 3 they retell in their own words, on two rows for each part, and write the lesson. For the lesson ask: "What did the characters learn? What can we learn?" Say it as something for people: "Share what you have." Day 1: retell aloud with a partner, then Level 1. Day 2: Level 2, and Level 3 for children who are ready. On screen, Juniper's Story Lantern tells a tiny fable and asks for its lesson.
note.watch: A retelling is right when the three parts are in order and the end is there. It does not have to match the key, and the word bank is a help, not a rule. On Level 3 accept any lesson that fits the whole story and tells people how to act. "Ben gave Fay plums" is a retelling: ask "So what does the story teach us?"

1:feeling-and-sense-words.title: Words That Show Feelings and Senses
1:feeling-and-sense-words.objective: Children find words in a story that tell how a character feels and words that tell how something looks, sounds, tastes, smells, or feels.

note.mistake: Children mix up how a character feels with what a thing feels like ("soft" is not a feeling). They give their own feeling instead of the character's. Some think only "happy" and "sad" are feeling words.
note.words: Open the Feelings Check-In tool and name the feelings and their faces together. Say: "A feeling word tells how someone feels inside: glad, mad, scared." Then: "A sense word tells what you see, hear, taste, smell, or touch: loud, sweet, soft." Touch your eyes, ears, mouth, nose, and hands as you name the senses. Read the story and stop at each of the four words: "Is this a feeling, or one of our senses? Which one?" On Level 1 the four words stand in a box: children underline them in the story and circle the face or the part of the body. On Level 2 they find the two feeling words themselves and answer a question about each sense word. On Level 3 they also tell how the other character feels and why.
note.watch: On Level 1 a feeling word gets a face and a sense word gets a part of the body. "Warm" and "soft" are felt with the skin: the hands stand for touch. On Level 3 any feeling word is right when the reason fits the story: "Ben feels sorry because Fay is hungry." Ask: "How do you know?"

1:who-tells-the-story.title: Who Is Telling the Story?
1:who-tells-the-story.objective: Children tell who is speaking at different points of a story: the narrator or one of the characters.

note.mistake: Children think the character named in a sentence is the one who says it: "Now Finn was glad" is told by the narrator, not said by Finn. Some skip the quotation marks, or think the words "said Fay" are spoken by Fay.
note.words: Say: "The narrator tells the story. The characters talk. Quotation marks show the words a character says out loud." Read one story as a play: one child plays each character and reads only the words inside the quotation marks, and you read the rest as the narrator. Then ask about single sentences: "Who says this? How do you know?" On Level 1 children circle the narrator or a character for six sentences. On Level 2 they write a letter in a box: N for the narrator or the first letter of the character's name. On Level 3 they also write one thing a character could say next. On screen, Lumen's Lighthouse Windows asks who is telling what was seen.
note.watch: Words inside quotation marks belong to a character, and the words "said Fay" belong to the narrator. On the page the spoken sentences are printed without "said ...", so each has one right answer. On Level 3 accept any words that fit the character and the end of the story; quotation marks around them are a bonus in Grade 1.

K:story-who-where.title: Who Is in the Story, and Where?
K:story-who-where.objective: Children tell who a story is about, where it happens, and one big thing that happens in it.

note.mistake: Children name every animal in the pictures instead of the one the story is about. For "where" they point to a thing ("the hat") and not to a place. For "what happened" they tell only the ending.
note.words: Read the story aloud twice: first straight through, then panel by panel while children touch each number. Teach three words with a gesture each: characters (point to yourself: who), setting (spread your arms: where), events (clap once: what happens). Ask: "Who is the story about? Where does it happen? What is one big thing that happens?" On Level 1 children circle a picture for each question. On Level 2 they draw the character, the place, and one thing that happens in three boxes. On Level 3 they draw in smaller boxes and write a word on the big row next to each drawing; writing the sounds they hear is fine ("lak" for lake). On screen, Dot's Story Spine asks for the start, the trouble, and the fix of a little story.
note.watch: A drawing is right when you can tell what it shows, or the child can tell you. Ask: "Who is this? Where is she?" If a child draws a helper (Frog for Duck), ask: "Whose hat is it? Who is the story about?" When the title names two animals (Bear and the Bee), or two animals do the work together (Rabbit and Hen), either one or both is right. On Level 1 the third row shows one pair of pictures from this story and two pairs from other stories.

K:retell-beginning-middle-end.title: Retell the Story: Beginning, Middle, End
K:retell-beginning-middle-end.objective: Children retell a story they have heard in order: what happens at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.

note.mistake: Children start with the part they liked best, or they tell only the end. Some name things ("a duck, a hat") instead of telling what happened.
note.words: Read the story aloud twice. Hold up three fingers and retell a story the class knows: "First ... Then ... At the end ..." On Level 1 children look at three pairs of pictures from the story and write 1, 2, and 3 to put them in order; then they tell the story to a partner with the pictures. On Level 2 they draw the beginning, the middle, and the end. On Level 3 they tell the story and finish three sentences that begin First, Then, and At the end, on big rows; a child may tell you the words to write, or write the sounds he or she hears. The telling matters more than the drawing: every child tells the story aloud once. On screen, Wake Up, Pip! lets children retell a story in order to a sleepy friend.
note.watch: A retelling is right when the three parts are in order and the end is there. Small details may be left out. The story has four panels and the page asks for three parts, so two panels may go together; on Levels 2 and 3 a beginning drawn from the first or second panel is right. This page prints the panels without numbers. If a child skips the middle, point to the second or third panel and ask: "What happened here?"

K:story-questions.title: Ask and Answer Questions About a Story
K:story-questions.objective: Children answer who, where, what, and how questions about a story they have heard, and ask a question of their own.

note.mistake: Children answer with something they know about the animal, not with what the story says. They mix up who and where. When asked for a question, they tell something instead ("The duck has a hat").
note.words: Read the story aloud twice. Read each question aloud and have children point to the panel that tells the answer before they circle a picture. On Level 1 the questions begin with Who and Where. On Level 2 they begin with What and How; a How question asks for a feeling, and children circle a face. On Level 3 children answer two questions and ask one of their own: they draw what they want to know, or they tell you the question and you write it in the box. Say: "A question asks something we want to know. It often starts with who, what, where, when, why, or how." On screen, Fable's Picture Stories gives more questions about three-picture stories.
note.watch: An answer is right when the story says it. Ask: "Which picture of the story shows that?" For a child's own question, accept any real question about the story, even one the story does not answer ("Why did Frog help?"). If the child tells a fact, say: "Turn it into a question. Start with who or what."

K:pictures-and-words.title: The Pictures and the Words
K:pictures-and-words.objective: Children match each part of a story they hear to the picture that shows it.

note.mistake: Children draw a line to the picture straight across from the sentence. They match by one thing they see (any picture with the cat) and not by what happens in the sentence.
note.words: This page prints the sentences of a story on the left and its pictures on the right, mixed up. Read sentence 1 aloud, have children put a finger on its dot, and ask: "Which picture shows this part? What do you see in it?" Then children draw the line. Say: "The pictures show what the words tell." On Level 1 there are three sentences (the first and the last of the story and one from the middle), on Level 2 all four. On Level 3 one picture is missing: children draw it in the empty box, then draw the line to it. Afterward, read the story again and let children point to each picture as its part is read. On screen, in Otto's Picture Book, children tap the picture that shows the part Otto reads.
note.watch: No picture stands straight across from its sentence, so a child who draws straight lines has not matched. Many pairs share an animal or a thing (the hat, Rabbit, the honey), so one picture is not enough. Ask: "Do you hear both things in this sentence?" On Level 3 the drawing is right when it shows who and what the sentence tells.

1:silent-e.title: Silent e Changes the Vowel
1:silent-e.objective: Children read and spell one-syllable words with a silent e and tell how the e changes the vowel sound: cap, cape.

note.mistake: Children read the silent e as a sound or keep the short vowel ("cap" for cape). In spelling they leave the e off (cak) or add it to every word. Some know a_e and do not carry the pattern over to i_e, o_e, and u_e.
note.words: Write cap on the board and read it. Add an e and say: "The e at the end is silent. It makes the vowel say its name: cap, cape." (Some programs call it magic e.) Do the same with kit and kite, not and note, cub and cube. With u the e can say two sounds: /yoo/ in cube and cute, /oo/ in tube. Children cover the e with a finger, read the short word, lift the finger, and read the long one. On the page they first add e to each word and read both words to a partner. Then they circle the word for each picture; the two words are a pair such as tap and tape, so only the vowel sound tells them apart, and at least two pictures show the short word. Level 1 has a_e words and two sentences, Level 2 a_e and i_e words and three sentences, Level 3 all four vowels and three words to write under pictures, with the first letter printed on each row. On screen, Add the Magic e lets children build the same kind of pairs.
note.watch: Listen to the reading, not only to the circles: a child can circle tape and still say "tap." In the sentences only one word of the pair makes sense ("A horse has a long mane."); have the child read the sentence aloud with the word chosen. On Level 3 a word with the right vowel and a final e is on the way: a child may write "noze" for nose; show the s that says /z/ and move on.

1:long-a-ai-ay.title: Long a: ai and ay
1:long-a-ai-ay.objective: Children read and spell one-syllable words in which ai or ay spells long a, and use the place in the word to choose between them.

note.mistake: Children write a alone (ran for rain) or a silent e for every long a (rane). They put ay in the middle of a word (trayn) or ai at the end (plai).
note.words: Say: "Two letters can work as a team and make one sound. A and i, and a and y, both say the name of a." Write rain and play. Ask where each team stands: "ai comes in the middle of a word. ay comes at the end." On Level 1 children draw a line from four words to their pictures, then write ai in four words and ay in four words and read them. On Level 2 they read eight printed words out loud and write each under its spelling, then read the rule and write ai or ay into six words. On Level 3 they cross out the one word of seven that does not say long a, write the other six under their spelling, write the word for three pictures, and finish two sentences with a word from a box. Have children read every finished word aloud. On screen, Build Vowel-Team Words lets them build long-vowel words from letter tiles.
note.watch: In the sort a word is right when it stands under its own two letters. In the Level 2 gap words the place decides: a gap at the end takes ay, a gap in the middle takes ai. Said has ai but does not say long a; it is a word to remember, and it is the word to cross out on Level 3. The Level 3 pictures are ai words (three of rain, train, snail, and nail), since few ay words can be drawn; the first letter is printed on each row, so a child who sees a rain cloud still writes rain. The word box holds two words that fit neither sentence.

1:long-e-ee-ea.title: Long e: ee and ea
1:long-e-ee-ea.objective: Children read and spell one-syllable words in which ee or ea spells long e.

note.mistake: Children write e alone (fet for feet) or mix the two teams (leef, seel). Unlike ai and ay, no rule tells which team a word takes, so children who look for a rule guess.
note.words: Say: "E and e, and e and a, both say the name of e. There is no trick for these two: we learn which words take which team." Sort a few known words on the board: see, tree, feet under ee; eat, sea, leaf under ea. See and sea sound the same; the team shows which one we mean. On Level 1 children match four words to pictures, then write ee in four words and ea in four words and read them. On Level 2 they read eight printed words out loud and sort them, then write ee or ea into six words that each have a picture. On Level 3 they cross out the one word of seven that does not say long e, sort the other six, write the word for three pictures (the first letter is printed on each row), and finish two sentences from a word box. Read the sorted columns aloud together at the end. On screen, Build Vowel-Team Words gives more practice.
note.watch: On Level 2 each gap word has a picture so the child knows the word; which team it takes cannot be heard, so it must be remembered. A child who writes "leef" has heard the sound and needs the look of the word: point to leaf on a word wall. ea can also say short e, as in head and bread; head is the word to cross out on Level 3. The Level 3 pictures are three of bee, tree, sheep, and leaf.

1:long-o-oa-ow.title: Long o: oa and ow
1:long-o-oa-ow.objective: Children read and spell one-syllable words in which oa or ow spells long o, and use the place in the word to choose between them.

note.mistake: Children write o alone (bot for boat) or a silent e for every long o (bote). They read ow as in cow in every word. They put ow in the middle (bowt) or oa at the end (snoa).
note.words: Say: "O and a, and o and w, can both say the name of o." Write boat and snow. "oa comes in the middle of a word. ow comes at the end." Tell children that ow has two sounds, as in snow and as in cow; on these pages it says the name of o in every word but cow. On Level 1 children match four words to pictures, then write oa in four words and ow in four words and read them. On Level 2 they read eight printed words out loud and sort them, read the rule, and write oa or ow into six words. On Level 3 they cross out the one word of seven that does not say long o, sort the other six, write the word for three pictures, and finish two sentences from a word box. On screen, Build Vowel-Team Words gives more practice.
note.watch: In the Level 2 gap words the place decides: a gap at the end takes ow, a gap in the middle takes oa. Words such as bowl and grown break this rule and are not on these pages. Cow has ow but does not say long o: it is the word to cross out on Level 3. Read row as in "row a boat." On Level 3 the pictures are three of boat, coat, goat, and toast, and the first letter on each row tells which name to write, so a child who says "ship" or "jacket" can still find the word.

1:ck-ng-wh.title: ck, ng, and wh
1:ck-ng-wh.objective: Children read and spell words with ck at the end (duck), ng at the end (ring), and wh at the start (whip), knowing each spelling makes one sound.

note.mistake: Children write k or c alone at the end ("duk," "soc"). They drop the g of ng ("rin") or say it as n and then g. They write w alone for wh ("wen").
note.words: Say: "A digraph is two letters that make one sound. c and k together make /k/ at the end of a short word: duck, sock. n and g together make the sound at the end of ring. w and h make /w/ at the start of when." Have children hum /ng/ with the mouth open. On Level 1 each copy works with ck or with ng, and a grey model starts each task: the child writes the digraph to turn five old words into new ones (dug, du__; wig, wi__), writes it into five more words, reads the new words to a partner, and circles the word that fits three sentences. On Level 2 children draw lines from four of six words to their pictures (two words, such as song beside sock, have no picture) and sort six words under ck and ng. On Level 3 wh joins: they write the word for three pictures, sort six words under ck, ng, and wh, and finish three sentences by writing the digraph. On screen, Build Blend and Digraph Words gives more practice.
note.watch: ck comes right after a short vowel at the end of a word. Before ng the vowel sounds a little different (ring, bang); teach -ing, -ang, -ong, -ung as chunks. In the ck sentences the other word ends in g (duck, dug), so the child must read to the end of the word. Most Americans say when and which with a plain /w/; some say /hw/, and both are fine. Levels 1 and 2 use no word that starts with a blend; truck and clock wait for Level 3.

1:blends-start.title: Blends at the start: st, fl, tr
1:blends-start.objective: Children read and spell one-syllable words that start with a consonant blend (stop, flag, trip) and say both sounds of the blend.

note.mistake: Children say or write only one sound of the blend: "top" for stop, "cab" for crab. Others put a vowel between the two sounds ("suh-top") or write the two letters in the wrong order ("tsop").
note.words: Say: "A blend is two consonants side by side. You hear both: s, t, st, stop." Stretch it, "sss-t-op," then say it fast. Pair words: top and stop, pin and spin. On Level 1 every copy is about s-blends, and a grey model starts each task: the child adds s to five old words to make new ones (top, _top), writes two given blends into two words each, reads the new words to a partner, and circles the word that fits three sentences; the other word is the same word without the s. On Level 2 children draw lines from four of six words to their pictures (two words, such as lag beside flag, have no picture) and sort six words under s-blends and l-blends. On Level 3 r-blends join: they write the word for three pictures, sort six words, and write the two letters that start a word in three sentences. On screen, Build Blend and Digraph Words lets them build blend words from letters. The page Blends gives more practice with pictures: on Level 1 the child circles the right two letters of three, on Level 2 writes them in front of the rest of the word (__og for frog), and on Level 3 names the picture and writes the two letters with no word printed.
note.watch: In an s-blend the s comes first (st, sp, sn, sk, sw, sm, sc); in an l-blend or r-blend the l or r comes second (fl, tr). sl is both an s-blend and an l-blend, so the pages leave it out. On Level 3 the sentences show no letters to choose from: the meaning tells the word ("A __ab walks on the sand": cr, crab). Have the child read the finished sentence aloud.

1:blends-end.title: Blends at the end: nd, mp, st, and nk
1:blends-end.objective: Children read and spell short-vowel words that end in a consonant blend (hand, jump, nest) and hear both final sounds.

note.mistake: Children leave off one of the last two sounds: "han" or "had" for hand, "jup" for jump, "nes" for nest. Before k they leave the n out ("sik" for sink). Some write the two letters in the wrong order ("hadn").
note.words: Say: "Some words end with two consonant sounds. Listen to the end: han-d, hand." Have children hold up a finger for each of the last two sounds. Compare had and hand, bed and bend. On Level 1 every copy is about nd, and a grey model starts each task: the child writes nd to turn five old words into new ones (had, ha__), writes nd into five more words, reads the new words to a partner, and circles the word that fits three sentences; the other word is missing a sound (sad, sand). On Level 2 children draw lines from four of six words to their pictures (two words, such as lap beside lamp, have no picture) and sort six words under nd and mp. On Level 3 st and nk join: they write the word for three pictures (hand, lamp, sink), sort four words under the four endings, and finish three sentences by writing nd, mp, st, or nk. On screen, Build Blend and Digraph Words gives more practice.
note.watch: In nk the n sounds like the end of ring: say sink slowly and feel the tongue move back before the k. Teach -ink, -ank, -unk as chunks. A child who writes "sigk" has heard that sound; show the n. In mp the lips close for m and pop for p. On Level 2 the four pictures are the same in every copy (hand, lamp, stamp, shrimp); the words change.

K:naming-and-action-words.title: Naming words and action words
K:naming-and-action-words.objective: Children sort pictured words into naming words (dog, cup) and action words (run, jump) and say each one in a sentence.

note.mistake: Children sort by what they see first: the card of a girl running goes to the naming box because it shows a girl. Some name an action card with a naming word (runner, dancer) and then sort it as one.
note.words: Say: "A naming word names a person, an animal, or a thing: doctor, dog, cup. An action word tells what someone does: run, jump." Hold up a ball and act out jumping; ask which one you can do. Day 1, Naming Words and Action Words: children cut out twelve cards and glue six in the naming box and six in the action box. On Level 1 the cards are pictures only, so name each card; the words to say are printed in small grey type at the foot of the Level 1 page, row by row. Level 2 prints the word under each picture; Level 3 is for children who read: the cards are words only, and children finish "The ___ can ___." Day 2, Find the Action Word: each row has one action and two naming words. On Level 1 name the three pictures in each row (one is a person standing still, such as a doctor or a farmer); the words to say are printed at the foot of the Level 1 page, row by row; children circle the action word. On Level 2 children read three short words and circle the action word. On Level 3 they read six sentences, circle the naming word, and underline the action word, as in the example at the top.
note.watch: For a card a child is unsure of, try it in "I can ___." "I can dog" makes no sense; "I can swim" does. Name each action picture with the action word: dance, not dancer; read, not book. A person is a naming word too: doctor and baby name who someone is, not what someone does. In the sentences, fast, big, little, and red are neither kind; only the naming word and the action word are marked.

K:capital-letter.title: A sentence starts with a capital letter
K:capital-letter.objective: Children find the capital letter at the start of a sentence and in the word I, and fix sentences that start with a small letter.

note.mistake: Children copy a sentence as it is printed and keep the small letter. Some write a capital at the start of every word, and many write the word I as a small i.
note.words: Write "the cat ran." on the board. Ask: "How does a sentence start?" Change the t to a T. Say: "A sentence starts with a capital letter. The word I is always a capital letter." Day 1, Fix the First Letter: each sentence is printed two ways, once with a capital and once with a small first letter. On Level 1 (three-word sentences) children circle the one written right; on Level 2 they circle it and write its capital letter in the box; on Level 3 every sentence starts with a small letter and children write its first word with a capital on the line. Day 2, A Sentence Starts with a Capital Letter: children circle the first letter of six sentences and each word I. Three sentences start with a small letter; for those, children write the capital in the box in front of the sentence. Level 1 has three-word sentences, Level 2 four- and five-word sentences, and Level 3 adds a sentence to copy on a line.
note.watch: The sentences have no names, so the only capitals are the first letters and I. On Day 1 the two ways differ in one letter only: have the child point to it. On Day 2 a child who writes a capital in every box has not looked; ask, "Does this letter look like the capital on our alphabet chart?" Check that the word I is circled inside a sentence too ("here I am").

K:period-or-question-mark.title: A period or a question mark?
K:period-or-question-mark.objective: Children name the period and the question mark, tell which one ends a telling sentence and which one ends an asking sentence, and add the right mark.

note.mistake: Children choose by the picture or by how long the sentence is, not by what it says. Some put a question mark only after a question that starts with what or where, and miss questions such as "Can a bee fly".
note.words: Draw a period and a question mark and name them. Say: "A telling sentence tells something and ends with a period. An asking sentence asks something and ends with a question mark." Read a pair aloud: "The dog can run. Can the dog run?" Ask which one asks. Day 1, Telling or Asking? Sort the Sentences: numbered strips, half telling and half asking, to cut out and glue under the period or the question mark. On Level 1 read each strip aloud the way you would say it; on Level 2 children read eight strips; on Level 3 they read six strips and write the mark at the end of each before gluing. Day 2, A Period or a Question Mark?: on Level 1 children circle the mark for six sentences you read; on Level 2 they read eight short sentences and write the mark in the box; on Level 3 they write the mark for four sentences, then one telling and one asking sentence about a picture.
note.watch: Every asking sentence on these pages starts with who, what, where, when, why, how, can, is, do, or does; point to the first word when a child is unsure. Half the sentences on a page tell and half ask. On Day 2, Level 3, a child may tell the two sentences while you write them; check the end marks.

K:make-the-sentence-longer.title: Say more: make the sentence longer
K:make-the-sentence-longer.objective: Children say a complete sentence about a picture, make it longer with words that tell where or when (The dog plays in the rain.), and write the words they added.

note.mistake: Children add words that do not fit the picture, or add a whole new sentence (The dog plays. It is raining.). When they write, some copy the short sentence again instead of the new words.
note.words: Show a picture and say a short sentence: "The cat sits." Ask: "Where? When?" Point to the sun, the moon, the rain, or the snow in the corner of the picture: "The cat sits in the sun." Say: "We can make a sentence longer. We add words that tell where or when." Each page has four pictures, and each shows one of these signs. On Level 1 read the sentence and its three choices; children circle the words that fit the picture. On Level 2 they circle the words and write them on the line. On Level 3 they write their own words on the line. Have each child read the whole long sentence aloud. On screen, Sunny-Side Diner has children say a whole order in one long sentence.
note.watch: The picture decides: a dog with snowflakes stands in the snow, not in the sun. On Level 3 accept any words that tell where or when and fit the picture (in the snow, outside, at night); the key gives one answer. Listen for one whole sentence when the child reads it back.

3:maps-diagrams-photos.title: Maps, Diagrams, and Photos
3:maps-diagrams-photos.objective: Children use a map or a diagram together with the words of a text to answer where, when, why, and how questions, and tell whether each answer came from the text, from the graphic, or from both.

note.mistake: Children answer from the words alone and skip the graphic, or look only at the pictures. They mark "text" because a place name is also in the text, even when only the map shows its square, or they mark "both" for every question. Some name a square the wrong way round (2B for B2) or give the direction from the wrong place.
note.words: Show a map or a diagram from a science or social studies book. Ask: "What does the text tell us that the picture does not? What does the picture tell us that the text does not?" Model one question of each kind: a square or a direction read off the map, a date or a reason read in the text, and one that needs both, such as "In which square did the Union Pacific Railroad start?" The text names the city; the map shows its square. Day 1 is the map page, day 2 the diagram page. On Level 1 children circle each answer and circle where they found it. On Level 2 they write each answer and put a check mark next to the source. On Level 3 they answer four questions; then they name the two places on the map that show only a number, or write what happens in the diagram step that shows a question mark.
note.watch: A question is "both" only when one fact comes from each source: the text tells which place or step, and the graphic gives its square, direction, or name, or the other way round. Ask: "Could you answer it with your finger on the map alone?" On the diagram page most step names, such as evaporation or mail carrier, are printed only in the diagram; the text tells in plain words what happens. Children may already know an answer (the president lives in the White House; lions eat zebras); ask where it is printed on this page.

1:long-or-short-vowel.title: Long or short vowel?
1:long-or-short-vowel.objective: Children say a one-syllable word, hear whether its vowel sound is long or short, and mark it.

note.mistake: Children go by the letter and not by the sound: every word with an a is "short a" to them. Others think a long vowel means a long word, or that a word with two vowel letters has two vowel sounds.
note.words: Say: "A long vowel says its name: a as in cake. A short vowel says its sound: a as in cat." Stretch the word, "caaake," and ask: "Do you hear the name of the letter?" On the page Long or Short Vowel? each card shows a picture and its word with the vowel in color. The child says the word and circles the line if the vowel sound is long and the curve if it is short. These are the marks teachers write over a vowel, a line for long and a curve for short; show them on the board over the a of cake and the a of cat. In cake, kite, and globe the e at the end is silent and not in color; it makes the first vowel say its name. Level 1 has six words, Level 2 has eight. On screen, Stretch the Giraffe has the child listen for long and short vowel sounds.
note.watch: Have the child SAY the word before marking it; a child who marks without saying the word is guessing from the letters. In boat and goat two letters are in color, and together they make one long o sound. Ask now and then: "Say the vowel sound alone. Is it the name of a letter?"

K:place-words.title: In, on top of, under, next to
K:place-words.objective: Children use the place words in, on top of, under, next to, above, between, behind, and in front of to tell where a thing is in a picture.

note.mistake: Children mix up above and on top of: a thing that is on top of another touches it, a thing that is above floats over it. Many point and say "there" and never say the place word.
note.words: Start with a real box and a toy: "Where is the bear? In the box. On top of the box. Under the box. Next to the box." Then hold the toy over the box without touching it: "Above. It does not touch." On the page Choose the Position Word each row shows a picture and a shape beside a sentence, and the child circles the one word of three that fits. Level 1 has in, on top of, under, and next to; Level 2 adds above and between; Level 3 adds behind and in front of. On a flat page, behind means the shape hides part of the picture, and in front of means the picture covers part of the shape; show this first with two paper cutouts. On day 2, on the page Read and Draw, read each sentence with the child ("The fish is under the square."); the child draws the fish where the sentence says, in the box with the shape. On screen, Bramble's Parking Tower gives more practice with above, below, next to, and between (below means the same as under).
note.watch: Ask the child to say the finished sentence aloud and to show it with a hand: "Show me under." On Read and Draw, look at where the drawing sits, not at how well it is drawn: on top of touches the shape, above floats over it.

2:short-or-long-vowel.title: Short or Long Vowel?
2:short-or-long-vowel.objective: Children tell short from long vowels when they read regularly spelled one-syllable words (hop and hope, step and steep, ran and rain) and sort printed words by the vowel sound.

note.mistake: Children read every vowel as short (hop for hope) and skip the silent e or the second letter of a vowel team (ran for rain). Some sort by looking for an e anywhere in the word instead of reading it, and put bed or step under long.
note.words: Write hop and hope. Say: "A short vowel says its sound: hop. A long vowel says its name: hope." Mark the vowels the US way: a breve over the o of hop, a macron over the o of hope, and cross out the silent e. Do the same with ran and rain, step and steep: the second vowel of a team is silent too. On Level 1 children circle the word for four pictures from two words such as cap and cape, sort six words under short vowel and long vowel, and circle the word that fits in two sentences. On Level 2 they sort eight words, half of them with blends and digraphs, and circle the word in four sentences. On Level 3 they sort six harder words and cross out the one word that is neither short nor long (car, star, park, cow, now, or boy), write the word for three pictures (the first letter is printed), and write the word that fits a sentence, choosing from the two words beside it. On screen, Add the Magic e builds the same short and long pairs.
note.watch: A child who sorts by sight alone puts bed under long because it has an e: have the child read the word aloud and listen for the vowel. In the sentences both words are real (cub and cube), so only the meaning tells which one fits; ask the child to read the sentence with the word chosen. On Level 3 a child may write bote for boat: both say long o, so point to the vowel team on the word wall.

2:vowel-teams-long-a-e-o.title: Vowel Teams for Long a, e, and o
2:vowel-teams-long-a-e-o.objective: Children read and spell one-syllable words with the vowel teams ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, and ow, and choose the team for a word: first by its vowel sound, then by its place in the word.

note.mistake: Children pick a team of the right sound in the wrong place (trayn, snoa), mix the two teams of long e (sleap, beech for beach), or hear the long vowel and write one letter (tran).
note.words: Review the three long vowels and their teams: "ai and ay spell long a. ee and ea spell long e. oa and ow spell long o." Then the places: "ai and oa come in the middle of a word: chain, float. ay and ow come at the end: spray, throw." On Level 1 each copy works on one long vowel: children write its two teams into six words (the rule is printed for long a and long o; for long e the line says that ee and ea say the same sound), write the word for two pictures (the first letter is printed), and finish two sentences from a box of four words. On Level 2 they sort six words of two long vowels by their sound, then write the team that makes a word in nine words, choosing among four teams. On Level 3 they choose among all six teams for six words, write the word for a long a, a long e, and a long o picture, and finish two sentences from a box. On screen, Build Vowel-Team Words and the vowel-team level of Word Doctor's Clinic give more practice.
note.watch: Both teams of a sound read the same, so reading aloud cannot show which is right. The rule decides between ai and ay, oa and ow. For ee and ea the child must know how the word looks: have them write it both ways and pick the one that looks right. On Level 2 the sound decides the column: rain and play both go under long a. Every ow on these pages says long o (snow, grow); cow and now come in the next lesson. The word box always holds two words that fit neither sentence.

2:vowel-sounds-oo-ou-ow-oi-oy.title: Vowel Sounds: oo, ou, ow, oi, and oy
2:vowel-sounds-oo-ou-ow-oi-oy.objective: Children read and spell words with oo (moon, book), ou and ow (cloud, cow), and oi and oy (coin, boy), and read them in sentences and riddles for meaning.

note.mistake: Children give every oo the sound of moon, even in book; read ow as long o in down and town; and put ou or oi at the end of a word (cou, boi).
note.words: Day 1, G2-532: say "oo can say two sounds: the sound in moon and the sound in book." Then: "ou comes in the middle of a word: shout. ow comes at the end: how. ow comes before a last n or l: town, howl. oi comes in the middle: soil. oy comes at the end: boy." Children sort words and write the team into words. Day 2, G2-543: the same spellings in sentences. Children circle yes or no ("A cow can bark."), write the answers to riddles (from a box; on Level 3 the first letter is on the line), and draw what a sentence says. On both pages Level 1 reads oo, Level 2 ou, ow, oi, and oy, and Level 3 all five.
note.watch: A child who answers yes to "A cow can bark." may have guessed from one word: have them read the whole sentence aloud. ow can also say long o (snow); these pages never use it that way. The word hoop is never sorted on Day 1: many say it with the oo of book. you is a heart word; its ou is not the ou of cloud.

2:bossy-r-ar-or.title: Bossy r: ar and or
2:bossy-r-ar-or.objective: Children read and spell words in which r changes the vowel, ar as in park and or as in storm, and read them in sentences and riddles for meaning.

note.mistake: Children read the vowel as short and add the r as a separate sound, drop the r in spelling (cat for cart), or write ar where or belongs (barn for born).
note.words: Day 1, G2-533: write cat and cart. Say: "Bossy r changes the vowel sound: ar says the sound in park." Then or: storm, fork, corn. Children match words to pictures, write ar or or into words, sort, and circle the word that fits a sentence. Day 2, G2-544: children circle yes or no ("A shark can swim."), write the answers to riddles (from a box; on Level 3 the first letter is on the line), and draw what a sentence says. On both pages Level 1 reads ar only, and Levels 2 and 3 read ar and or.
note.watch: Words like war, warm, word, and work look like these but say other sounds; they are not on these pages. A child who writes barn for born hears the r but not the vowel: read both words aloud and ask which one fits.

2:er-ir-ur.title: er, ir, and ur: One Sound, Three Spellings
2:er-ir-ur.objective: Children read words with er, ir, and ur, which say the same sound (her, first, turn), check which spelling a word uses, and read the words in sentences and riddles.

note.mistake: Children spell the sound with the one spelling they know best (berd, shurt) or with r alone (brd), and stop checking because the word sounds right.
note.words: Day 1, G2-534: say "er, ir, and ur say the same sound: her, first, turn." Children write er into words, sort words under er, ir, and ur, circle the spelling that looks right, and write words for pictures. Day 2, G2-545: children circle yes or no ("A cat has fur."), write the answers to riddles (from a box; on Level 3 only the first letter is on the line, so the child chooses er, ir, or ur), and draw what a sentence says. On both pages Level 1 reads er only, and Levels 2 and 3 read er, ir, and ur.
note.watch: Praise checking, not hearing: when a child is unsure, have them write the word two ways and pick the one that looks right. here, there, and where have the letters but not the sound; they are crossed out on Day 1 and are not on the Day 2 page.

2:long-vowels-two-syllable-words.title: Long vowels in two-syllable words
2:long-vowels-two-syllable-words.objective: Children split two-syllable words that have a long vowel in one syllable (rainbow, cupcake, paper), read each syllable, and read the words in sentences.

note.mistake: Children read the first vowel as short (pap-er for paper), split a compound word in the wrong place, or guess a long word from its first letters.
note.words: Write rain | bow and say "A compound word splits between its two small words." Then cup | cake: "A silent e at the end makes the vowel long." Then pa | per: "When a syllable ends with a, e, i, o, or u, the letter says its name." On G2-546 children draw a line between the two syllables of twelve words, circle each syllable with a long a, e, i, o, or u, and circle the word that fits in six sentences. On G2-547 they finish six words from a first part and a part from a box (rain + bow), then circle yes or no for sentences. Level 1 has compound words with a vowel team, Level 2 words with a silent e, Level 3 words whose first syllable ends with its long vowel.
note.watch: Some words have two long syllables (oatmeal, pinecone, photo): circle both. Do not circle a second syllable with a quick weak sound (paper, tiger, open, bacon). In playground only play is long: ground's ou is not a long vowel. Have the child read each part aloud, then the whole word.

2:tricky-words-could-would-should.title: Tricky words: could, would, should
2:tricky-words-could-would-should.objective: Children read and spell could, would, should, because, and friend by mapping the sounds they know and learning the tricky part by heart.

note.mistake: Children spell the words the way they sound (cud, wud, becuz, frend), or leave out the silent l of could, would, and should.
note.words: Say: "Some words have a part that does not follow the rules. We learn that part by heart." Write could in sound boxes: c, oul, d. The c and the d say the sounds children know; oul says the oo of book, and the l makes no sound, so it gets a heart. would and should work the same way: one heart over oul. In because the heart goes over au, in friend over ie. On the page children write the letters for each sound in a box and draw a heart over the tricky part; then they write the heart word that fits a sentence, with its first letter on the line. Levels 2 and 3 add again, any, many, people, does, or other: the heart goes over ai, a, a, eo, oe, o. Level 1 has four words (could, would, should, and because or friend) and four sentences; Level 2 six words and three sentences; Level 3 six words, one sentence, and a sentence of their own with two heart words from the page. On screen, Heart Words runs the same routine of sound boxes, a heart, and writing. Its first shelf (the, of, to, do, was, said, you, have, come, some) is open to everyone, with the whole routine and the printable word cards, and a teacher can type any word and show it to the class (the list is not kept). The Teacher plan adds the other eleven shelves, among them could, would, should, friend, and because; a saved list of her own words; and the wall and take-home sheets.
note.watch: A dashed line marked "Fold back" runs under the words: on Levels 2 and 3 the child folds the top back and writes the sentences from memory, then unfolds it to check. The heart goes over the tricky letters only: the c and d of could keep their usual sounds.

K:short-a-i.title: Short a and short i
K:short-a-i.objective: Children say the short sounds of a and i and read and spell CVC words with them, such as cat, map, pig, and sit.

note.mistake: Children say the letter's name, not its sound ("ay" for a). Others read the first letter and guess the rest, so "ham" becomes "hat," or they read "him" as "ham" because they skip the vowel. When they spell, a and i get mixed up.
note.words: Say: "Short a says /ă/, as in apple. Short i says /ĭ/, as in igloo." Model blending: touch each letter, say its sound, then say the sounds fast: /k/ /ă/ /t/, cat. Day 1, Short a and Short i: on every level children read six words and draw a line from each word to its picture. Two words have no picture; each differs from a pictured word only in the vowel (hat and hit), so children must read the middle letter. If a child does not know a picture, look at the six words together: the picture's word is one of them. Level 1 practices short a: the four pictures are short-a words, and children write a in six words, starting from the grey example, and read the new words to a partner. Level 2 mixes a and i: after the match, children read four words aloud and write each one under a or i, crossing out each word as they write it. Level 3: after the match, children write the word for three pictures; the first letter is printed on the line, and one picture is the pig. Day 2, Build the CVC Word: children build CVC words from letters on screen and read each word they build.
note.watch: Listen for the vowel. A child who reads "him" as "ham" is reading the first and last letters only: cover the word, uncover one letter at a time, and have the child say each sound. When a child writes "bg" for bag, stretch the word together (/b/ /ă/ /g/) and ask, "What do you hear in the middle?" Before n and m, the a in can, fan, and ham sounds a little different; it is still short a, spelled a.

K:short-o-u-e.title: Short o, short u, and short e
K:short-o-u-e.objective: Children say the short sounds of o, u, and e and read and spell CVC words with them, such as hot, bug, and bed.

note.mistake: Children mix up short o and short u (hot and hut) and short e and short i. They often spell short e with an i, especially before n or m: in many US homes pen and pin sound the same.
note.words: Say: "Short o says /ŏ/, as in octopus. Short u says /ŭ/, as in umbrella. Short e says /ĕ/, as in elephant." Have children say each sound with you: /ŏ/: drop your jaw, as for the doctor's "ahh." /ŭ/: a short, relaxed "uh." /ĕ/: open your mouth a little less than for /ă/. Day 1, Short o, Short u, and Short e: on every level children read six words and draw a line from each word to its picture; two words have no picture and differ from a pictured word only in the vowel (pot and pit). If a child does not know a picture, look at the six words together: the picture's word is one of them. Level 1 practices one vowel; each copy uses o or u. Children write the vowel in six words, starting from the grey example, and read the new words to a partner. Level 2 uses two of the three vowels: after the match, children read four words aloud and write each under its vowel. Level 3 uses all three: children write the word for three pictures, one with each vowel; the first letter is printed on the line. Day 2, Build the CVC Word: children build CVC words on screen and read each word they build.
note.watch: The pages keep e and i apart: no task asks a child to hear the difference between e and i before n or m, and no sort puts e against i. When a child spells pen with an i, show the printed word and say, "This word uses e." In some homes dog and log sound a little like "dawg"; accept the child's way of saying them and keep the spelling o.

K:change-one-sound.title: Change one sound to make a new word
K:change-one-sound.objective: Children change the first, last, or middle sound of a spoken CVC word to make a new word (cat to hat, hat to ham, ham to him) and spell each new word.

note.mistake: Children change the wrong sound: asked to change /t/ in cat to /p/, they say "pat." Others say a rhyming word instead of making the change. When they spell, some write a new word from scratch and change two letters. The middle sound is the hardest to hear.
note.words: Model with letter tiles: "Say cat. Change /k/ to /h/. What is the new word? Hat." Swap the tile so children see that one letter changes and the rest stay. Day 1, Change One Sound: each page is a ladder of six words. Before you copy the page, cut off the teacher strip at its foot and keep it: it holds your steps. Read the top word together; it is printed with its picture. Then read the steps on your strip, one at a time ("2 change /k/ to /h/"). Children write the new word on the next step and read it; say the new word together before the next change. When the new sound is /k/, the step line names the letter, c or k. Level 1: only the first sound changes; the last two letters are printed in grey to trace, and children write the first letter. Level 2: the first or the last sound changes, and children write the whole word in the three boxes. Level 3: the first, middle, or last sound changes. Day 2, Pepper's Sound Swap: children change one sound on screen to make a new word.
note.watch: Before each change, have the child point to the box of the sound you named. A child who writes two new letters has started over: read the word on the step above and ask, "Which sound changed?" Every word on the ladder is a real word, and no step changes e and i before n or m (pen, pin), which sound alike in many homes.

K:words-one-letter-apart.title: Which word matches: cat or cot?
K:words-one-letter-apart.objective: Children tell apart two words that differ by one letter (hat and hot, bag and big) by saying the sound of the letter that differs and choosing the word for the picture.

note.mistake: Children circle the word that starts like the picture's name without reading the rest. Others look at the picture, say its name, and circle any word of the right length without reading the letter that differs.
note.words: Write hat and hot on the board. Say: "These words look almost the same. One letter is different." Read both words with the children, point to the a and the o, and say their sounds: /ă/, /ŏ/. Day 1, Which Word Matches?: each page has ten pictures (eight on Levels 2 and 3), each with two words that differ in one letter. Children read both words, circle the word for the picture, and underline the letter that is different in the word they circled. Level 1: the first letter differs (cat and bat). Level 2: the last letter differs (cat and can). Level 3: the middle letter, the vowel, differs (hat and hot). Day 2, Bingo's Word Hunt: children read look-alike words on screen and tap the one that names the picture.
note.watch: Ask the child to say the sound of the letter that differs in each word; a child who can circle the word but not say the sounds is guessing from the picture. Level 3 never pairs e and i before n or m (pen and pin), which sound alike in many US homes. Every picture is one most kindergartners name with its word; if a child calls a picture something else, have the child read both words: only one of them names the picture.

1:capitals-names-days-months.title: Names, days, and months get capitals
1:capitals-names-days-months.objective: Children capitalize the names of people and pets, the days of the week, and the months in sentences and in dates.

note.mistake: Children give a capital to every word about a person or a time: my Mom, my Dog, Day, Summer. Others leave a name small in the middle of a sentence.
note.words: Say: "A name starts with a capital letter: Mia, Rex. The days of the week and the months do too: Monday, June. Words like mom, dog, day, and summer do not." Point to the calendar. Day 1, Capital Letter or Small Letter?: each sentence prints one word two ways; children circle the right one. Level 1 has names, Level 2 adds the days, Level 3 the months. Day 2, Names, Days, and Months Get Capitals: names, days, and months are printed small; children circle each one and write each one again on the row below. Then they write the date and their first and last name; Level 3 adds "My birthday is in ___."
note.watch: Mom gets a capital when it is used as her name: Thank you, Mom! After my it stays small. Seasons stay small. On Levels 1 and 2 children copy the date from the board.

1:joining-words.title: Joining words: and, but, so, because
1:joining-words.objective: Children join two short sentences with and, but, so, or because and choose the joining word that makes sense.

note.mistake: Children choose and for every pair, because and can join any two sentences. Others mix up so and because and write "It snowed because we made a snowman."
note.words: Say: "A joining word puts two sentences together. And adds one more thing. But tells something you did not expect. So tells what happened because of it. Because tells why." Read a pair with each word and ask which fits best: "The sun is out but it is cold." The box at the top of the page says what each word does. Level 1 uses and and but: children circle the word in five sentences, then join two sentences and write them as one. Level 2 adds so. Level 3 uses all four words, and children write a sentence of their own with because. When children join two sentences, the first period goes and the second sentence starts with a small letter: The bird can sing and it can fly. Or joins two choices (Do you want milk or juice?): practice it aloud. On day 2, Hazel's Word Bridge has children tap the joining word that fills the blank.
note.watch: And can join almost any two sentences; it fits best only when the second sentence adds one more thing of the same kind. So comes before what happened because of it; because comes before the reason. A sentence with because needs both parts: not "Because it is cold." Grown-up writing usually puts a comma before and, but, or so when it joins two sentences; children learn that comma in Grade 4, so accept either.

1:verb-tense.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: verb tense
1:verb-tense.objective: Children use verbs to tell about the past, the present, and the future (Yesterday I walked. Today I walk. Tomorrow I will walk.).

note.mistake: Children add ed to every verb, even after tomorrow ("Tomorrow I will walked"), or leave out will. Some copy the form from the next column without reading the time word.
note.words: Say: "A verb tells when. Yesterday I walked. Today I walk. Tomorrow I will walk." Write the three forms of one verb under Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow. The table on the page has the same three columns, and one form of each verb is missing. On Level 1 a worked row in grey comes first, and children add ed to write the yesterday form of three verbs. On Levels 2 and 3 the missing form can be in any column. Below the table on Levels 1 and 2, children read four sentences and circle the verb that fits the time word: yesterday, last night, or last week; tomorrow or tomorrow night. On Level 3 children choose one of three verbs and write about it after Yesterday I, Today I, and Tomorrow I. Start with the page; on day 2, The Clock Tower has children read the time word in each sentence on screen and tap the verb that fits.
note.watch: Every verb on these pages adds ed with no change in spelling. The ed says /t/ in walked, /d/ in played, and /id/ in painted. The sentences tell about yesterday or tomorrow, so the plain verb never fits them; ask, "When did it happen?" and point to the time word first. On Level 3, "Today I am calling my friend" is right too.

2:prefixes-un-re.title: Prefixes un- and re-
2:prefixes-un-re.objective: Children tell the meaning of a word formed when un- or re- is added to a known word (happy and unhappy, tell and retell).

note.mistake: Children read the base word and skip the prefix: they circle fair for "not fair" or write fold for "fold again." Some mix the two prefixes up and write retie for "the opposite of tie."
note.words: Say: "A prefix is a word part at the start of a word. It changes what the word means. un- means not or the opposite of: unhappy means not happy, and unlock is the opposite of lock. re- means again: retell means tell again." Write happy on the board, add un-, and read both words. Day 1, the page. Level 1 (un- only): children add un- to words and write each new word (a done example in grey, then 3 more), circle the word that means "not fair" or "the opposite of fold" among three words in five rows, and circle the word that fits in three sentences; sometimes the word without un- is the one that fits. Level 2 (un- and re-): children read two meanings (not safe, fold again) and write the new word, draw lines from four words of two base words (untie, retie, unload, reload) to their meanings, and write un or re in the gap of three sentences. Level 3 adds pre-, which means before: two meanings to write, three sentences with un, re, or pre, and one sentence of their own that uses both words from part 1. Day 2, Marigold's Knowing Machine on screen: children read a built word and tap what it means. pre- is on the page only.
note.watch: Have children read a sentence with each word before they choose: "Hold my hand so you stay unsafe" sounds wrong. The base word never changes its spelling: un + tie, re + fill. Every gap on Levels 2 and 3 takes a prefix, so the child reads the whole sentence to know which one fits. Some words only look as if they start with un- or re- (uncle, under, ready): take the letters away and no word is left.

2:suffixes-ful-less-ly.title: Suffixes -ful, -less, and -ly
2:suffixes-ful-less-ly.objective: Children read words with the suffixes -ful, -less, and -ly (helpful, careless, slowly) and say what the suffix adds.

note.mistake: Children read the suffix as a word of its own (care full) and spell -ful with two l's (carefull). In a sentence some write careful where the sentence needs careless, because they read only the base word.
note.words: Say: "A suffix is a word part at the end of a word. -ful means full of: helpful means full of help. -less means without: careless means without care. -ly tells how: slowly means in a slow way." Write help on the board, add -ful and then -less, and read the three words. Day 1, the page. Level 1 (-ful only): children circle the base word and underline -ful in six words (a done example in grey, then 5 more) and read each word to a partner, read meanings (full of skill) and write the -ful word (a done example in grey, then 3 more), and circle the word that fits in four sentences: the base word or its -ful word. Level 2 (-ful and -less): children mark six words, draw lines from four words of two base words (careful, careless, painful, painless) to their meanings, and write ful or less in the gap of three sentences. Level 3 adds -ly: children mark six words and cross out the one word that has no suffix, match four words, and write ful, less, or ly in three sentences. Every gap takes a suffix. Day 2, Marigold's Knowing Machine on screen: children read a word with -ful or -less and tap what it means; -ly is on the page only.
note.watch: The suffix -ful has one l: careful. On these pages the base word keeps its spelling: care + ful, safe + ly. Some words only look as if they had a suffix (jelly, belly, silly, fly, bless): take away -ly or -less and no word is left (jel, bel, sil, f, b). Ask "How?" for an -ly word: How did the turtle crawl? Slowly.

2:apostrophes.title: Apostrophes: can't and the dog's bowl
2:apostrophes.objective: Children use an apostrophe to write contractions (can't, it's, we're) and common possessives (the dog's bowl).

note.mistake: Children put the apostrophe where the two words meet instead of where the letters are left out (do'nt), or leave it out (dont). For an owner some write dogs with no apostrophe, or put an apostrophe in every word that ends in s.
note.words: Say: "An apostrophe takes the place of letters that are left out: do not becomes don't, and the apostrophe stands where the o was. An apostrophe and s also show who owns something: the dog's bowl is the bowl that belongs to the dog." Day 1, the page. Level 1 (contractions only): children write contractions from their words (a done example in grey, it is → it's, then 5 more), draw lines from four contractions to the two words they stand for (two first words, such as we and they, so both parts must be read), and write the two words for three contractions. Level 2 adds owners: three contractions to write, three to write the two words for, and owners with a thing, each a picture or a child's name printed with its word, to write as dog's bowl or Mia's kite (a done example in grey, then 3 more). Level 3: six contractions, three to write and three to write the two words for, two sentences (The kite belongs to Mia.) to write as Mia's kite, and four sentences with one missing apostrophe: children write that word with its apostrophe. Day 2, Nib's Apostrophe Seat on screen: children read two words and choose the contraction with the apostrophe in the right place. Owners with 's are on the page only.
note.watch: The contraction can't is short for cannot. The contraction won't (will not) changes its spelling; it is not on the pages. Every owner on these pages is one owner. The word its, with no apostrophe, stands only on Level 3: "Its time for bed" needs it's. When the word to fix starts a sentence, accept a lowercase first letter.

1:syllable-vowel.title: Every syllable has a vowel
1:syllable-vowel.objective: Children count the vowel sounds in a printed word to find how many syllables it has, and mark the vowel in each syllable.

note.mistake: Children count letters instead of vowel sounds, or guess by length. On Level 3 of day 2 they count vowel letters, not sounds: cake and rain get two.
note.words: Say: "Every syllable has a vowel sound. Find the vowels and listen for them: fish has one; nap | kin has two." Day 1: children underline each vowel in twelve words, write 1 or 2, and match four of six words to pictures. Two words have no picture (rock beside rocket, picnic beside pretzel). Level 1 uses short words and compound words (sandbox); Level 2 two-syllable words like napkin; Level 3 adds a line between the two syllables, between the two consonants: bas | ket. Day 2: children sort six words under 1 syllable or 2 syllables and circle the two-syllable word in each of five sentences. On Levels 1 and 2 every word has one vowel letter for each vowel sound. Level 3 has eight words and four sentences and adds silent e and vowel teams: "Count the vowel sounds, not the vowel letters: cake has one, cup | cake has two."
note.watch: Have children read each word aloud after counting: the vowels and the beats must agree. A long word can have one syllable (plants). In many two-part words the second vowel is quiet (kit | ten); it still makes a beat. These pages use no y on its own as a vowel (baby, my), no r after a vowel (carpet), and no word like wheel or smile, which many children clap as two beats.

1:compound-and-two-part-words.title: Compound words and two-part words
1:compound-and-two-part-words.objective: Children read two-syllable words by breaking them into parts, starting with compound words (sunset, cupcake) and then words like rabbit and picnic.

note.mistake: Children read the first part and guess the rest (sand for sandbox), or split in the wrong place: rabb | it, s | andbox. Some think every long word is two small words and call kitten kit + ten.
note.words: Say: "A compound word is two small words put together: sun + set = sunset. Read each part, then the whole word." Write sandbox, cover box, read sand, then uncover it. Day 1, the page: on Level 1 children draw a line between the two small words of ten short-vowel compound words, then write the two small words of two compounds (such as egg and shell) and draw a picture of each. Level 2 adds compounds with a long vowel (snowman, beehive) and words with a double consonant, split between the two letters (rab | bit), with the same writing and drawing task. On Level 3 children split eight words, now also words like bas | ket, and sort six words under compound word or not a compound word, crossing out each word as they write it. Day 2, on screen: the screen activity Domino's Two-Part Words shows a word in two parts (rab · bit); the child reads each part, blends them, and pushes the word to its picture. The next lesson splits more words into syllables.
note.watch: In many compound words both parts keep their meaning: a sandbox is a box of sand, a lunchbox is a box for lunch. Some take a new meaning (catfish, laptop). The Level 3 sort uses only the first kind. Kitten and napkin look like two small words but are not compounds, so the Level 3 sort never uses them. When a child splits a word wrong, have them find the two vowel sounds first: each part has one.

1:tricky-words-said-was-of-could.title: Tricky words: said, was, of, could
1:tricky-words-said-was-of-could.objective: Children read and spell common irregular words (said, was, of, could, and review words such as they and put) by mapping the regular sounds and remembering the tricky part.

note.mistake: Children sound out the tricky part and spell what they hear: sed, wuz, uv, cud. Others write the regular letters wrong because they try to remember the whole word as a picture.
note.words: Say: "Most of said follows the rules: s says /s/, d says /d/. The ai is the tricky part; here it says /ĕ/. We learn that part by heart." Say each word, tap its sounds, write the letters for each sound, and put a heart over the part the rules do not give. On screen, the tool Heart Words runs the same routine of sound boxes and a heart; said, was, and of are on its first shelf, and a teacher can type could, fix where its sounds break, and mark its heart. Then the page: children say each sound, write its letters in a box, draw the hearts, fold the top of the page back, and write the heart word that fits each sentence. Level 1 has said, was, of, and could and four sentences, with the first letter of each answer on its line; Level 2 adds two words from they, does, friend, put, and give and has three sentences; Level 3 mixes six words in three columns, has one sentence with no first letter, and asks the child to open the page again and write a sentence of their own with two heart words. they, does, friend, put, give, and come are review words: model where their hearts go before Level 2 or 3.
note.watch: The tricky parts: ai in said, the a of was, oul in could (the l is silent), ey in they, oe in does, ie in friend, the u of put, the ve of give, the o and the final e of come. In of both letters are tricky: the tool puts its heart on the f only; on the page both letters get one, because the o says /ŭ/. The s of was and does says /z/ as in is and has; that is a rule, not a heart. Never ask a child to sound out the tricky part: say it.

3:closed-open-syllables.title: Closed and open syllables
3:closed-open-syllables.objective: Children divide two-syllable words into closed and open syllables (rab | bit, ro | bot, cam | el) and read each syllable with the right vowel sound.

note.mistake: Children split every word after the first vowel and read camel as ca | mel ("KAY-mel"), or split after the consonant and read robot as rob | ot with a short o.
note.words: Say: "A closed syllable ends with a consonant, and its vowel is short: nap | kin. An open syllable ends with a vowel, and the vowel says its name: ro | bot." Day 1, Closed and Open Syllables: children split sixteen words, write C or O in a box for each syllable, and circle the word that fits each of six sentences. Level 1 words have two consonants between the vowels (rab | bit, hip | po); Level 2 words start with an open syllable (ro | bot, so | lo), plus three or four Level 1 words; on Level 3 one consonant stands between the vowels, so children try the long vowel first and then the short one. Day 2, Closed or Open?: children write each word under its head with a line between the syllables, then circle yes or no. Level 2 adds words like cam | el; on Level 3 one word fits neither head (oven, many) and is crossed out.
note.watch: The boxes under a word do not show where the line goes. Digraphs stay together (dol | phin, ech | o), and a blend after a long vowel goes with the next syllable (pro | gram). Ask, "Is ca | mel a word? Is cam | el?" In a second syllable the vowel is often said quickly (ba | con, lem | on, kit | ten); it is still a closed syllable.

3:syllable-types-e-team-le.title: Silent-e, vowel-team, and consonant-le syllables
3:syllable-types-e-team-le.objective: Children find silent-e, vowel-team, and consonant-le syllables in longer words (cupcake, rainbow, table, puzzle) and read the words part by part.

note.mistake: Children split before the l of a consonant-le word (tab | le) and read a short a, or read the silent e of cupcake as a sound.
note.words: Say: "A consonant-le syllable is a consonant plus le. Count back three letters: ta | ble, bum | ble | bee. A silent e makes the vowel before it long: cup | cake. A vowel team is two or more letters that spell one vowel sound: rain | bow." Day 1: children split twelve words (nine on Level 3) and write each syllable's type in its box: C closed, O open, E silent e, V vowel team, L consonant-le (printed on the page); then they write ten words (twelve on Level 3) under their heads. Level 1 has consonant-le words, sorted by a short or long first vowel; Level 2 adds silent-e words and sorts by the type of the last syllable; Level 3 splits three-syllable words (bum | ble | bee) and sorts into three types. Day 2, Build Long Words: children find the box part that makes a word with each first part, write the part and the whole word, then circle yes or no for eight sentences.
note.watch: Words with ck before le (pickle) split after the ck; none is on these pages. The Level 1 sort leaves out oo words (noodle): oo does not say the name of o. Each first part makes a word with one box part only.

3:suffixes-able-ment-ness-ful-less.title: Suffixes -able, -ment, -ness, -ful, -less
3:suffixes-able-ment-ness-ful-less.objective: Children decode words with common suffixes (washable, payment, kindness, careful, endless) and tell how the suffix changes the base word.

note.mistake: Children read the base and drop the suffix, mix up -ful and -less, or keep the y and the e when they spell (happyness).
note.words: Say: "-ful means full of, and -less means without. -ness and -ment turn a word into a noun: soft, softness. -able means can be." Day 1, Base Words and Suffixes: children circle the base and underline the suffix in twelve words, match four words to their meanings (two words of one base, such as careful and careless, so the suffix decides), and add a suffix to a base word to finish five sentences. Level 1 has -ful and -less, Level 2 adds -ness and -ment, and Level 3 has all five, with bases that change: after a consonant, y changes to i (happiness), and a silent e is dropped before -able (lovable). Day 2, Which Word Fits?: children circle the word that fits each of seven sentences (two words of one base), then build three words and write what each means.
note.watch: A silent e stays before a suffix that starts with a consonant (hopeful, movement), and a y after a vowel stays: playful, payment, enjoyable. The key's meanings are samples: accept "not careful" for careless.

3:tricky-words-enough-though-ocean.title: Tricky words: enough, though, ocean
3:tricky-words-enough-though-ocean.objective: Children read and spell grade-level words with irregular spellings (enough, though, ocean, laugh, through) by mapping the regular parts and remembering the tricky part.

note.mistake: Children sound out ough letter by letter, or spell by sound alone (enuf, tho, oshun).
note.words: Say: "Most of a heart word follows the rules. We learn the tricky part by heart." Map enough on the board: e | n | ou | gh, and draw a heart over ou and gh. Day 1, Heart Words: children write the letters for each sound in a box and draw a heart over the tricky part; a silent letter shares a box with the letter beside it (sl in island, sw in answer), and ough gets one box where it spells one sound (though, through). Then they fold the words back and write the heart word for each sentence; on Level 1 its first letter is on the line. Level 1 has four words and six sentences, Level 2 eight words and six sentences, Level 3 six words, four sentences, and a sentence of the child's own. Enough, though, and ocean are on every page. Day 2, The Sounds of ough: read the words together, then children write each one under the sound its ough makes (uff, o, or aw) and circle yes or no for five or six sentences.
note.watch: Don't sound out o-u-g-h letter by letter; teach ough as one unit and try its sounds (uff, o, aw). The e of enough says a quick /i/. On Level 3 one word (through or drought) has another ough sound and is crossed out.

3:joining-words.title: Joining words: and, but, so, because, when
3:joining-words.objective: Children choose a joining word (and, but, or, so, because, when, if, after, before) that shows how two ideas go together, and write the joined sentence with a comma where one belongs.

note.mistake: Children use and for everything. Many mix up so and because: so comes before the result, because before the reason. Some put a comma before because.
note.words: Say: "A joining word shows how two ideas go together. And adds an idea, but shows a difference, or gives a choice, so tells the result, because tells why." Day 1, Choose the Joining Word: the child circles the word that fits and writes it in the blank, with a comma in front of and, but, or, or so; the sentences print no comma, so it never gives the answer away. Level 1 offers two words (and, but, so); Level 2 adds or and because and offers three; Level 3 adds when, if, after, and before, and offers a second word of that group that does not make sense. Day 2, Join Sentences: the child joins four pairs (three on Level 3) on two lines each, circles the word, then finishes sentences that end in a joining word. The key names every word of the box that joins a pair right.
note.watch: It was raining, so we played inside. We played inside because it was raining. A comma goes before and, but, or, and so when they join two sentences. If the part with because, when, if, after, or before comes first, put a comma after it: When it gets dark, owls hoot. And joins almost any two sentences: ask which word shows how the ideas go together best.

3:simple-compound-complex.title: Simple, compound, and complex sentences
3:simple-compound-complex.objective: Children tell simple, compound, and complex sentences apart and build compound and complex sentences from two short sentences.

note.mistake: Children call every sentence with and or a comma compound, even "Mia and Leo built a snow fort." Others call any long sentence complex, or leave out the comma of a compound sentence.
note.words: Say: "A simple sentence is one complete thought with a subject and a verb. A compound sentence is two sentences joined by a comma and a joining word: and, but, so, or. A complex sentence is a sentence plus a part that cannot stand alone; the part starts with because, when, if, after, or before." Day 1: the child checks the kind of each sentence; Level 1 sorts ten into simple and compound (two simple ones have a list with commas), Levels 2 and 3 twelve into all three kinds, and Level 3 adds simple sentences with two subjects or two verbs and one like "We played outside after lunch." Day 2, Build: each sentence gets two lines; Level 1 joins six pairs, Level 2 writes three pairs both ways, Level 3 one pair both ways and a paragraph rewritten as two compound sentences and one complex sentence.
note.watch: To test a compound sentence, cover the joining word: two sentences are left. To test a complex sentence, read the part with because, when, if, after, or before alone: it cannot stand by itself. If that part comes first, put a comma after it: When it gets dark, owls hoot. The keys give one right sentence; other joins are right if they keep the meaning.

3:comparing-adjectives-adverbs.title: Better, best: comparing with adjectives and adverbs
3:comparing-adjectives-adverbs.objective: Children form and choose comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs (taller, tallest; more carefully, most carefully; good, better, best) and choose an adjective or an adverb by what it tells about.

note.mistake: Children add -er to long words (carefuller), use both (more taller), use -est when only two things are compared, say gooder, or write biger and happyer.
note.words: Say: "Compare two things with -er or more, and look for than. Compare three or more with -est or most, and look for the." Words with one syllable take -er (tall, taller); most longer words take more (careful, more careful); good, bad, well, and badly change. Show the spelling moves: big, bigger, biggest (double the last letter) and happy, happier, happiest (y becomes i). Day 1: the child circles one of three forms under each sentence; Level 1 has -er and -est words, Level 2 adds more and most, Level 3 has good, bad, well, and badly, and three sentences that ask for the adjective or the adverb. Day 2: the child writes the form of the word in ( ) in four sentences about three animals drawn at three sizes, then both forms of six words in a table (Level 2 mixes -er and more words; Level 3 adds words that change).
note.watch: Than means two: taller than. The ... of the three, of all, or in the world means three or more. Very, too, and as ... as take the word itself: very big. An adverb tells how someone does something: Tess painted carefully; Tess is careful.

3:possessive-nouns.title: Possessives: the dog's bone, the dogs' bones
3:possessive-nouns.objective: Children write singular and plural possessives (the dog's bone, the dogs' bones, the children's coats) and tell a possessive from a plural that owns nothing.

note.mistake: Children put an apostrophe in every word that ends in s (three dog's ran). Others always write 's, even when more than one owner ends in s, or write childrens'.
note.words: Say: "Count the owners. One owner: add 's, the dog's bone. More than one owner, and the plural ends in s: add an apostrophe after the s, the dogs' bones. A plural that does not end in s takes 's: the children's coats. A plural that owns nothing needs no apostrophe." Day 1, Possessive Nouns: the child writes who owns it for six owners ("Two dogs have bones." the dogs' bones), then circles the word that fits in four sentences; Level 1 has one owner only, Level 2 adds more than one owner, Level 3 adds plurals such as children, men, women, mice, and geese. Day 2, Add the Apostrophe: the child writes the underlined word the right way (some need none). On Level 1 the child decides by whether something owned follows the word; on Levels 2 and 3 a first sentence says how many there are.
note.watch: Ask "How many owners?" before the apostrophe goes in. If no thing follows the word, it owns nothing: Three dogs ran. On these pages the number is said in words or shown by the sentence.

3:capitals-in-titles.title: Capitals in titles
3:capitals-in-titles.objective: Children capitalize the first word, the last word, and the important words of book, story, and song titles, and keep small words such as a, the, and, of, and in small.

note.mistake: Children capitalize every word, or only the first one. Some leave the first word small when it is a small word (the Lost Lantern).
