note.words: Say: "In a title, the first word, the last word, and every important word start with a capital letter. Small words like a, the, and, of, and in stay small in the middle." The box on every page lists the small words. Day 1, Find the Capitals: the child circles each word that needs a capital in titles printed in small letters, then circles the right one of a title printed two ways; Level 1 has three-word titles, Level 2 titles with a, the, of, and in, Level 3 titles with a name or a colon. Day 2, Capitals in Titles: the child writes each title with its capitals, then the titles of three books he or she likes and a title for a report.
note.watch: Is, are, and it are short but important words, so they always get a capital. Words such as from, about, into, and with are left out of these titles because style guides disagree on them. A name always gets a capital, and so does the first word after a colon: Leo and the Lighthouse: A Summer Story. All the titles are made up.

1:words-by-category.title: A duck is a bird that swims: words by category
1:words-by-category.objective: Children sort words into categories and define a word by category and key attribute (a duck is a bird that swims).

note.mistake: Children say what a thing does, not what kind it is ("a duck swims"), or sort by where it lives: a frog goes with the fish.
note.words: Say: "A definition tells what kind of thing it is and what makes it special. A duck is a bird that swims." Day 1: children cut out the cards and glue each in its category's box. Level 1 has two boxes, Level 2 birds, fish, and insects. On Level 3 each box says what its members have (Birds have feathers.); two cards fit no box and get an X. The X cards are two of: bat, frog, spider, snail, worm, starfish. Day 2, on screen first: in Olive's Kind-Of Tree — What Kind of Thing Is It? (Grade 1) children climb a picture to the branch of its kind. Then, on Levels 1 and 2, children copy the category into three frames and circle the words that finish two definitions. Read each sentence and its three choices aloud with the class: the task is choosing, not decoding. On Level 3 they write a category from the box and a special thing for two pictures.
note.watch: A picture may not show every leg: every insect has six. A penguin's feathers are short and tight; a bat flies but has no feathers. On Level 3, accept any true special thing, and "an animal" or "a food" before asking for the smaller group.

1:endings-s-ed-ing.title: Endings -s, -ed, and -ing
1:endings-s-ed-ing.objective: Children read and write words with -s, -ed, and -ing (jumps, jumped, jumping) and find the base word in each.

note.mistake: Children read jumped as "jump-ed" or skip the ending; on Level 3 they keep the silent e (bakeing) or forget to double (naping).
note.words: Say: "An ending changes a word: help, helps, helped, helping. The base word is still there. On Level 3 it may double its last letter (hopping) or drop its silent e (baking)." Day 1, on screen first: in Build Words with Endings — Reading -s, -ed, and -ing children tap where the base word ends and pick the ending a sentence needs. Then the page: children circle the base word in six words and write base words with -s, -ed, and -ing in a table. Level 1 starts with a row done in grey; Level 2 adds -es (dress, dresses) and one word with no ending to cross out; Level 3 has two such words, a word that doubles its last letter, and one that drops its silent e. Day 2, Levels 1 and 2: children circle the word that fits each sentence, then add an ending to a base word in a box. Level 3: they finish Yesterday I, Now I am, and I can see two with a word from a box.
note.watch: A box on the day 2 page names the clue words. The -ed says /t/ in jumped, /d/ in played, /id/ in rested. The pages use only words that add -ed (never ran or went). If a child writes went or ran, it is good English; ask for a word that adds -ed.

3:context-clues.title: Context clues
3:context-clues.objective: Children use the sentence, and the sentence after it, as a clue to the meaning of a new word: a definition, a synonym, an antonym, or examples.

note.mistake: Children guess from how the word looks, or they take the clue word itself as the meaning when the clue is an opposite (calm for turbulent).
note.words: Say: "A context clue is a hint near a new word. A definition tells what it means. A synonym means almost the same. An antonym means the opposite. Examples show what it means." Signal words help: is, or, which means (definition); such as, like, including (example); but, unlike, while, instead of (antonym). Day 1, What Kind of Clue?: children underline the clue, write D, S, A, or E in the box, and give the meaning. Level 1 has six sentences with definition and antonym clues; Level 2 has eight, two of each kind; on both, children circle the meaning. On Level 3 they write it. Day 2, Context Clues in a Passage: six words are bold in a short text. On Level 1 each clue is a definition in the same sentence, and children circle one of three meanings. On Level 2 the clues are examples and opposites, and children write the meaning. On Level 3 the clue is in the next sentence, and children write its kind and the meaning.
note.watch: Have children read the sentence again with their meaning in place of the bold word: does it make sense? With an antonym clue, the meaning is the opposite of the clue. The key's written meanings are samples.

3:dictionary-glossary.title: Use a dictionary and a glossary
3:dictionary-glossary.objective: Children use guide words to find words in a print dictionary and a glossary, choose the right meaning, and check a spelling.

note.mistake: Children compare only the first letters of guide words, or they take the first meaning of a word without reading its sentence.
note.words: Say: "Guide words are the first and last words on a dictionary page. A word is on that page if it comes between them in ABC order. If the first letters match, look at the next letter." If one word is the start of the other (cap, cape), the shorter word comes first. Day 1, Use a Dictionary: a page of twelve entries; children circle the guide words of the page a word is on, the meaning a sentence uses, the right spelling, and more. On Level 1 the first letter decides the page; on Level 2 the guide words share a first letter; on Level 3 the third letter decides the page, and children write an entry for a new word. Day 2, Use a Glossary: a science text and its glossary. Children circle yes or no for sentences the glossary proves and write the two words a new word goes between. On Level 1 each glossary word has its own first letter; Levels 2 and 3 add words from other pages of the book, so a later letter decides. On Level 3 one bold word is missing, and children write its entry.
note.watch: A glossary gives the meaning a word has in that book; a dictionary may give more than one. A class may also look a word up in an online children's dictionary.

3:parts-of-speech.title: What each word does in a sentence
3:parts-of-speech.objective: Children explain the job of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs in general and in particular sentences, and label them.

note.mistake: Children label a word by how it looks, not by its job: every word that ends in -ly becomes an adverb (friendly, lonely), and is or was is left out because it shows no action.
note.words: Say: "A noun names a person, animal, place, or thing. A pronoun takes the place of a noun. A verb shows an action or a state of being: am, is, are, was, were. An adjective describes a noun. An adverb describes a verb. It tells how, when, or how often." Day 1, Sort the Parts of Speech: children write each word in the column of its job and cross it out, then write two words of their own for each job. Level 1 sorts nouns, verbs, and adjectives only. Day 2, Label the Parts of Speech: children write N, P, V, Adj, or Adv in the box under each word; a, an, and the are grey and get no label. Level 1 uses N, V, and Adj only. Level 3 uses longer sentences and ends with a sentence of the child's own that uses all five jobs: the sentence on the first line, its labels on the second.
note.watch: Ask "What does this word do here?" before a child writes a label. On Level 3 both pages have adverbs with -ly, an adjective with -ly (friendly, lonely), and an adverb without -ly (often, never), so the ending alone does not decide. Every verb to sort is a past form, so it cannot be read as a noun, and at least half are irregular (ran, ate), so -ed does not give the verbs away.

3:plural-nouns.title: Plural nouns: regular and irregular
3:plural-nouns.objective: Children form and use regular plurals (boxes, babies, leaves) and irregular plurals (mice, teeth, children) in sentences.

note.mistake: Children add -s to every noun (foxs, babys, wolfs) or add an ending to an irregular plural (childrens, feets). Some keep the y after a consonant (ladys).
note.words: Say: "Most nouns add -s. Nouns that end in s, x, z, ch, or sh add -es. After a consonant, y changes to i and we add -es: baby, babies. Some words that end in f or fe change the f or fe to v and add -es: leaf, leaves. Irregular nouns change in their own way or stay the same: mouse, mice." Day 1, Which Plural Is Right?: children read twelve sentences and circle the right plural; the other choices are the singular or common misspellings (sheep stays the same). Day 2, Plural Nouns: children write the plural of sixteen nouns and the number of the rule they used, then write the plural of the noun in ( ) in six sentences. Level 1 uses rules 1 and 2, Level 2 rules 1 to 4, and Level 3 all five rules.
note.watch: A word that ends in a vowel and y just adds -s: key, keys. Not every word with f changes: these pages use only words that do. Deer and sheep stay the same; fish is not on these pages.

3:past-tense-verbs.title: Past tense: regular and irregular verbs
3:past-tense-verbs.objective: Children form and use the past tense of regular verbs (jumped, carried) and common irregular verbs (ran, brought, knew).

note.mistake: Children add -ed to an irregular verb (runned, bringed) or skip a spelling move (hoped for hopped, carryed). When they rewrite a story, they change the first verbs and leave later ones in the present.
note.words: Say: "A regular verb adds -ed. If it ends in e, add -d. If it has one syllable, one short vowel, and one consonant at the end, double the last consonant (never x). A verb that ends in a vowel and y just adds -ed: play, played. If it ends in a consonant and y, change y to i. An irregular verb changes in its own way: go, went." Day 1, Past Tense: on Level 1 every verb is regular, and children write the past tense and the number of its spelling move; Levels 2 and 3 mix in irregular verbs, and children circle R or I. Six sentences that name a time in the past follow. Day 2, Rewrite the Story: on Levels 1 and 2 every verb is underlined and numbered, and a small box repeats the spelling moves; children write each past form, then the first three sentences in the past tense. On Level 3 nothing is underlined: children find the verbs and rewrite the whole story.
note.watch: Read the story aloud first. Each verb in it has one past form, and the Level 1 stories have regular verbs only. Never double x (mixed, relaxed); a verb of two syllables such as visit or open just adds -ed. Verbs that look the same in the past, such as read and put, are never asked.

3:subject-verb-agreement.title: Subjects and verbs agree
3:subject-verb-agreement.objective: Children make the verb agree with its subject (The dog runs. The dogs run.) and the pronoun agree with the noun it stands for.

note.mistake: Children make the verb agree with the nearest noun (The box of crayons are) and use is after two subjects joined by and. A pronoun may not match its noun (The puppies played. It rolled.).
note.words: Say: "When the subject is one, the verb usually ends in s: runs, is, was, has. When the subject is more than one, it does not: run, are, were, have." Day 1, Subjects and Verbs Agree: children circle the verb that agrees and draw an arrow from it to its subject. Level 1 puts the subject next to the verb, and its box says that I and you take the verb without s: I have, you are; Level 2 puts words between them; Level 3 has two subjects joined by and, There is and There are, and pronouns that agree with a noun in the sentence before. Day 2, Fix the Words That Do Not Agree: children cross out the verb or pronoun that does not agree and write the right word on the line; on Levels 2 and 3 two sentences are already right and get a check mark. Then children write two sentences of their own.
note.watch: Have children find the subject first and put a finger on it. In a There sentence, the subject comes after the verb. When two things do the action, the arrow points to both: the key underlines the whole subject.

2:words-in-real-life.title: Spicy, juicy, crunchy: words in real life
2:words-in-real-life.objective: Children connect describing words to real things and places they know (foods that are spicy or juicy, places that are noisy) and use them in sentences.

note.mistake: Children pick a thing they like instead of one the word describes (spicy: ice cream), or a word that goes with another word of the sentence: for "The lunchroom is ___ when we all talk," some circle crunchy because of lunch.
note.words: Say: "A describing word tells what a real thing is like: how it tastes, feels, looks, or sounds. An orange is juicy." Teach calm (quiet and still: a still pond) and gloomy (dark and sad-looking: a rainy day) first. Day 1, G2-549. Level 1: circle the picture each word describes; three sentences. Level 2: match six words to pictures (one picture is left over); two sentences. Level 3: circle the two things each word describes; three sentences. Day 2, G2-550. Level 1: draw or write two real things for four words; finish two sentences (A juicy fruit is ...). Level 2: four words, then a sentence of their own. Level 3: four words, then a riddle with two of them (I am prickly and juicy. What am I?).
note.watch: Tastes differ, so on day 2 accept any food a child calls spicy. The key's things and sentences are samples: accept any real thing the word describes, not one it does not (a juicy rock); ask the child why. On day 1 no picture, thing, or sentence goes with two words of its page; some go with none (the picture left over on level 2).

2:adjective-or-adverb.title: Adjective or adverb?
2:adjective-or-adverb.objective: Children tell adjectives from adverbs and choose between them to describe a noun or a verb (a quick dog, the dog ran quickly).

note.mistake: Children choose the -ly word because it looks longer and harder, or the shorter word every time. Some draw the arrow to the next word, even when the word it tells about stands before it (The lion is loud: loud tells about lion).
note.words: Say: "An adjective tells about a noun: a slow turtle. An adverb tells about a verb, how it is done: the turtle walked slowly. Many adverbs end in -ly." Ask: "Does the word tell about a person or thing, or about how someone did something?" Day 1, the page: the child circles the word that fits and draws an arrow from it to the word it tells about. Level 1: five sentences with pictures, then four words to sort. Level 2: six sentences, then short frames (a ___ boy, asked ___). Level 3: four sentences with good and well, then two of their own. Day 2, Glim's Describing Words — Adjectives & Adverbs on screen: children tap the word that fits; after a wrong tap, Glim says whether the blank tells about a thing or an action.
note.watch: On the page an adjective stands before its noun (a soft pillow) or after is, are, was, or were; on screen it also comes after looks or felt (The kitten looks sleepy) and still tells about the noun. An adverb stands before its verb or at the end (smiled kindly). The level-1 sort can be done by the -ly ending alone; the sentences show who chooses by meaning. happy changes y to i before -ly (happily); the page that holds it prints the rule. good tells about a noun and well tells how something is done: "sings good" needs well. Words with no -ly form (fast, hard, late) are not on the pages, and loud, slow, and quick never stand where "talk loud" could be said. The key's own sentences are samples: accept any where the adjective tells about a noun and the adverb about a verb.

K:book-parts.title: Front cover, back cover, and title page
K:book-parts.objective: Children find and name the front cover, the back cover, and the title page of a book and show where the story starts.

note.mistake: Children call the title page the front cover, because both show the title. Some think the back cover is the last page of the story.
note.words: Hold up a picture book and say: "The front cover shows the title, the author, and a picture. Inside, the title page shows the title and the author again. The story starts after it. Turn the book over: this is the back cover. The back cover often tells about the book and has a bar code." Day 1, K-665: read the box on the page with the class. Level 1: two books, each drawn as its three parts; children circle each front cover and put an X on each back cover. Level 2: children cut out three labels, glue each under its part, and circle the title on the front cover and on the title page. Level 3: a fourth part, the first page of the story, gets no label; children put a green dot on it (either page of that open book is right). Day 2, K-666: children make their own front cover and title page. They trace the title (Levels 1 and 2) or copy it from the big title above the row (Level 3), draw a picture, and write their name after by: they are the author.
note.watch: Ask, "How do you know this is the front cover?" A child who points to the title and the picture knows; a child who points to any book shape is guessing. A front cover has its spine on the left, a back cover on the right. The titles and authors are made up.

K:left-to-right.title: Read left to right, top to bottom
K:left-to-right.objective: Children follow printed words from left to right, top to bottom, and page by page while the teacher reads, pointing to each word.

note.mistake: Children start in the middle of a line, or at its end they stay on the line instead of sweeping back to the left. In an open book they read the higher words first, even on the right page.
note.words: Use a big book or chart: point under each word and sweep back to the left. Say: "We start at the left and read to the right. Then we go back to the left and down to the next line." Day 1, K-667: sentences of four to six words run over two lines, each on a page that ends just after the first line. Level 1: a green dot marks the start and a red dot the end; children trace the arrow under each line and the arrow back to the next line while you read. Level 2: nothing is printed; children put the green and the red dot and draw the arrows. Level 3: children write 1, 2, 3 ... in the box under each word. Day 2, K-668: pattern-book pages (I see a cow.). Level 1: two pages; children number the three lines and dot the first and the last word of each page. Level 2: a book of four pages as two open spreads; children write the page numbers in the circles and dot the first and the last word of the book. Level 3: two open spreads; children number the four lines of each.
note.watch: On Level 3 of K-668 at least one spread has its right page's lines higher than its left page's. A child who writes 1 on the highest line reads top first: ask, "Which page do we read first?"

K:spoken-written-words.title: One spoken word, one written word
K:spoken-written-words.objective: Children match each word they say in a short sentence to one written word on the page, pointing word by word.

note.mistake: Children touch a word for each beat, so caterpillar gets four taps and they run out of words before the sentence ends. Some think one letter or a scribble is a word.
note.words: Write a short sentence on chart paper; say it and touch one word at a time; clap a long word and show it is still one word. Say: "Each word we say is one word on the page." Day 1, K-669: children circle the word in each row. Then read each sentence slowly while they touch each word and put one dot under it. Level 1: three words of one beat. Level 2: four or five words, one or two of two beats. Level 3: a word of three beats or more. Day 2, K-670: say the name of each picture; children circle the word that fits. A word that takes longer to say usually has more letters. Have children clap the word before they choose (Level 2). Level 1 gives two words, Level 2 three. Level 3: for each picture, read the sentence the teacher strip names; the children point to the words; you do not. Cut the strip off before you copy the page.
note.watch: A child who ends on the last word before you finish has tapped beats: touch the words together again. On K-670 you name each picture, so no child has to guess its name.

K:spaces-between-words.title: Spaces between words: count the words
K:spaces-between-words.objective: Children find the spaces that separate printed words, count the words in a sentence, and leave a finger space when they copy one.

note.mistake: Children count beats or letters instead of words, or count the spaces and forget the last word. When they write, they run the words together.
note.words: Write a sentence on chart paper without spaces, then with finger spaces; ask which is easier to read. Say: "A space comes between two words. We count the words, not the claps." Day 1, K-671: four sentences in big print with wide spaces. Children draw a line in each space, count the words, and circle the number (Level 1: two or three words, each space marked with a dotted box) or write it in the box (Level 2: three to five words; Level 3: four to six words). On Levels 2 and 3 a sentence always has more beats than words. Day 2, K-672: each row shows a sentence with spaces and the same sentence without them; children circle the one that is easy to read. Then they cut out big word cards and glue them in the order of the sentence above, a finger space between them: three cards on Level 1, four on Level 2, five on Level 3. Level 3 also has a short sentence to copy on a writing row with finger spaces.
note.watch: Have children put a finger after each word as they glue or write. A child who writes 4 for The rabbit hops. is counting beats: touch each word and count again.

3:opinion-and-reasons.title: State an opinion and plan the reasons
3:opinion-and-reasons.objective: Children tell an opinion from a fact, find the opinion, the reasons, and the conclusion in a short opinion piece, and plan their own piece: an introduction, an opinion, three reasons with a fact or an example each, and a conclusion.

note.mistake: Children give a fact as their opinion, or a reason about something else. Some call an example a reason. I like summer is a fact about the speaker, not an opinion.
note.words: Model first: read one piece aloud, underline the opinion, and ask of each sentence: Does it tell why? Say: "An opinion tells what you think. People can disagree with it. A fact can be checked. A reason tells why, and an example shows that the reason is true." Day 1, Opinions and Reasons: fact or opinion for six sentences; then the child marks the opinion, the reasons, and the conclusion of a short piece and writes one more reason. Levels 2 and 3 plant a sentence about something else, which the child crosses out; on Level 3 the reasons have no signal words and part 1 asks: Can it be checked? Day 2, Plan Your Opinion Piece: the child circles one of two questions and fills the planner (a frame, a starter, or a label word on each line, by level), then checks the plan, conclusion included. The small plan on the page is on another question.
note.watch: A true fact about something else is still no reason. A fact can use a word like tallest (The giraffe is the tallest animal.): it can be checked, so it is a fact. Keep each child's plan: the draft in the next lesson starts from it.

3:linking-words.title: Reasons with linking words
3:linking-words.objective: Children connect an opinion and its reasons with linking words (because, since, therefore, for example) and draft an opinion piece that uses them.

note.mistake: Children use because where therefore belongs, or put For example before a new reason instead of an example. Many leave out the comma after Therefore or For example.
note.words: Model first: join "Tag is fun. Everyone can play." two ways on the board (Tag is fun because everyone can play. Since everyone can play, tag is fun.). Say: "Because and since tell why. Therefore tells what happens as a result. For example gives an example." Day 1, Choose the Linking Word: six blanks; the child circles the word that fits, then joins two opinions with their reasons. Because and since are never offered together. Days 2 and 3, Draft: children need their plan from the lesson before. Day 2: the introduction and reasons 1 and 2; day 3: the rest, then a rereading with the checklist in the margin. On Levels 1 and 2 the draft has no conclusion yet: it is written in Write a Conclusion (part 3). Level 3 drafts the whole piece, conclusion included.
note.watch: Since it was cold, we stayed in: a sentence that starts with since or because needs both parts and a comma between them. Therefore and For example start a sentence and take a comma after them.

3:concluding-statement.title: End with a concluding statement
3:concluding-statement.objective: Children tell a concluding statement from a new reason and from a sentence that changes the subject, and write conclusions that say the opinion again in new words.

note.mistake: Children end with a new reason, with The end., or with the opinion copied word for word.
note.words: Model first: read a piece and its opinion aloud, then say the opinion again in new words on the board. Say: "A concluding statement comes at the end. It says your opinion again in new words. It does not give a new reason, and it does not change the subject." Day 1, Find the Conclusion: three short pieces, each with three endings; the child circles the concluding statement (Level 1) or writes C, R, or X next to each ending (Levels 2 and 3). Day 2, Write a Conclusion: a better ending for a piece with a weak one, an ending for a piece with none, and the conclusion of the child's own draft. Level 1 prints the frame That is why, Level 2 a starter, Level 3 open lines and a word bank. Part 3 needs the child's draft from the lesson before.
note.watch: Read the ending with the opinion: it should say the same idea in other words. It may start with That is why, but it does not have to.

3:revise-and-edit.title: Revise and edit an opinion piece
3:revise-and-edit.objective: Children edit a paragraph for capitals, end marks, commas, a missing linking word, and a sentence that does not belong, then revise their own piece with a checklist and a partner.

note.mistake: Children cross out a sentence they do not like instead of the one that does not belong, or change words that are right.
note.words: Model first: "Revise: add a reason, an example, a conclusion. Edit: capitals, end marks, commas, spelling." Say: "Writers read their work again. They fix what is wrong and make it better." Day 1, Edit an Opinion Paragraph: the box names each kind of mistake, how to fix it, and how many there are (four on Level 1; Level 2 adds a missing comma after For example; Level 3 a word-wall word spelled wrong). Then children write each sentence they fixed. Day 2, Revise Your Opinion Piece: two worked examples (one content change, one mark fix), a checklist for the child and a partner, a partner's comment, and one sentence to add (Level 3: one change the child made). Children need their draft and its conclusion from the lessons before.
note.watch: Each mistake has one fix. Where the blank takes since, accept because too (and the other way round). With no word wall, use the class spelling list. The sentence that does not belong is about something else (My pencil is green.).

3:plan-a-story.title: Plan a story: characters, setting, problem
3:plan-a-story.objective: Children establish a situation and introduce a narrator or characters, and plan an event sequence that unfolds naturally to an ending.

note.mistake: Children plan events that have nothing to do with the problem, or an ending that does not solve it. In a story told by "I" they leave the narrator out of the characters.
note.words: Model first: read a story beginning aloud, then plan one idea aloud on the board. Say: "The beginning of a story tells who is in it, where and when it happens, and what goes wrong." Day 1, The Parts of a Story: children read a story beginning and answer who, where and when, and what goes wrong. Level 1 has three questions with three answers to circle; Level 2 adds "Who tells the story?", and some stories are told by a character who says I; on Level 3 children write all four answers. Day 2, Plan Your Story: children circle one story idea and write short notes for the characters, setting, problem, three events, and ending, with an example from another idea beside each part. Level 1 gives a starter for every part, Level 2 for the events and the ending, Level 3 a word bank. Children keep the plan for the time-words lesson.
note.watch: Each wrong answer names a person, a place, a time, or a trouble that is not in the story: send a child back to the text. Words inside quotation marks are a character talking: an I there does not make that character the narrator. In a plan, check that each event leads to the next one and that the ending solves the problem.

3:dialogue-and-description.title: Dialogue and description
3:dialogue-and-description.objective: Children use dialogue with quotation marks and descriptions of actions, thoughts, and feelings to show how characters respond to events.

note.mistake: Children put quotation marks around the whole sentence or the comma outside the closing mark. Many tell a feeling instead of showing it.
note.words: Model first: write "We won," said Kim. on the board and circle the exact words; then turn Nell was cold into what Nell does. Children need their story plan. Say: "Quotation marks go around the exact words a character says. The comma, question mark, or exclamation point goes inside the closing mark." Day 1, Quotation Marks in Dialogue: three speech bubbles, each with three sentences to circle, then two lines to write with their marks. On Level 1 the choices say the bubble's words in different ways; on Levels 2 and 3 only the marks differ, and Level 3 puts the speaker first in some lines. Day 2, Show Feelings in a Story: Level 1 circles the sentence that shows a feeling and writes dialogue on frames; Level 2 rewrites two telling sentences with an action and uses a said-word from a box; Level 3 rewrites one with an action and a thought. Said is fine in dialogue; in revising we change it when a more exact word fits.
note.watch: Ask: "Which words did the character say out loud?" The marks go around just those words. A question keeps its question mark, and then there is no comma. A thought may also go in quotation marks: He thought, "What is that?" When a child writes "she felt sad," ask what she did.

3:time-words-in-stories.title: Time words that order the events
3:time-words-in-stories.objective: Children use temporal words and phrases (later that day, after a while, finally) to signal the order of events and write a sense of closure.

note.mistake: Children start every sentence with then or and then. Some use finally for an event in the middle, or jump back in time (the night before) in a story told in order.
note.words: Model first: read a short story aloud, underline its time words, and tell its events again in order; then write one event of your own plan with a time word. Children need their story plan and their lines of dialogue. Say: "Time words tell when things happen and help a reader follow the order." Day 1, Time Words in a Story: children number the events of a short story from their time words (Level 1 four, Level 2 five, Level 3 six); the time words give one order. Then they circle the time word that fits a blank in tiny stories. Day 2, Write with Time Words: children read an example story and write their own under the headings beginning, middle, and ending, with two lines for each event, one line of dialogue, and one sentence that shows a feeling. Level 1 starts the story with One day, and each event with a time word; Level 2 gives a row of time words; Level 3 a word bank.
note.watch: To number events, have children find the first and the last event first. Read a draft aloud and listen for and then in every sentence. An ending tells how the problem is solved, not just The end.

3:words-for-effect.title: Revise for words that work
3:words-for-effect.objective: Children revise their story by choosing words and phrases for effect, replacing weak words (went, said, nice) with exact ones.

note.mistake: Children pick the fanciest word, not the one that fits (stared at the clock for just a second). Some change the meaning when they change a word.
note.words: Model first: read The dog went to its bowl aloud, try raced, crept, and wandered in its place, and say which one paints the picture you mean. Children need the story draft they wrote in the time-words lesson. Say: "Said, went, looked, nice, big, and good are tired words. A more exact word paints a clearer picture." Day 1, Choose a More Exact Word: four sentences with an underlined tired word and three words to circle; exactly one fits. On Level 1 the wrong words are of another kind; on Level 2 one wrong word is of the same group, but a clue in the sentence rules it out; on Level 3 both are. Then children circle the sentence that paints a clearer picture and write why. Day 2, Revise for Words That Work: a story with eight tired words and a box of more exact words for each. Level 1 underlines four and offers two words for each; Level 2 underlines all eight; on Level 3 children find them. Last, they circle three tired words in their own draft and write the sentences again.
note.watch: Ask: "Which words in the sentence help you choose?" On Day 2 more than one word of the box can fit; the key names them all. Only the six words in the box count as tired words. A new word must keep the meaning of the sentence.

3:take-notes-and-sort.title: Take notes and sort them
3:take-notes-and-sort.objective: Children take brief notes from short print sources, keeping the key words, and sort the notes under headings.

note.mistake: Children copy whole sentences, or write a note that changes the fact. When they sort, some put a note under the first heading it reminds them of.
note.words: Children need: finding the main facts of a short text. Model first: turn one sentence into a three-word note that keeps its key words, and sort three notes under two headings. Say: "A note is a few words about one fact. We do not copy whole sentences. We keep the key words." Day 1, Choose and Sort Notes: for each sentence children circle the best note; one choice copies the sentence and one changes a fact. Then they write the number of each note about another topic under its heading: six notes and two headings on Level 1, nine and three on Level 2. On Level 3 they write their own note for one sentence, and one of ten notes fits no heading and is crossed out. Day 2, Take Notes and Sort Them: on Level 1 children copy the words in bold from Source A under their headings; on Level 2 they take notes from Sources A and B with the letter of each; Level 3 adds a heading of their own.
note.watch: Ask, "What is this note about?" before a child sorts it. A good note keeps the fact true: check it against the sentence. On Day 2 the notes in the key are samples; accept any short, true note with its source letter. If both sources give a fact, either letter is right. On Level 3 accept any heading that names the leftover facts.

3:introduce-and-group.title: Introduce a topic and group the facts
3:introduce-and-group.objective: Children write an introduction that names the topic and group related information together, with a picture that helps the reader.

note.mistake: Children start with one fact, or with a question the piece never answers. When they group, some put a note under a heading because of one shared word.
note.words: Children need: sorting notes under headings (Take notes and sort them). Model first: write two openings for a few notes (one fact, one about the whole topic), ask which tells what the piece is about, and name a group of notes. Say: "An introduction tells what the whole piece is about. A heading names a group of facts that go together." Day 1, Introductions and Groups: for two model topics children circle the best introduction; the others are a detail, a sentence about another topic, and on Levels 2 and 3 a question the notes do not answer. Then they head each group of notes from the box; on Levels 2 and 3 one heading is left over, and on Level 3 one note in the wrong group is crossed out. Day 2, Plan Informative Writing: children write an introduction and each note under its heading, draw a picture with a caption, and tick the check list. Level 1 prints the headings and starts the introduction and the caption; Level 2 gives three heading words; Level 3 four.
note.watch: Ask: does it name the topic and tell about all of it, or only one part? The detail is a true fact, so a child may like it best; point to the headings it leaves out. On Day 2 the key is a sample; accept others that fit the notes.

3:facts-definitions-details.title: Facts, definitions, and details
3:facts-definitions-details.objective: Children develop each part of an informative piece with facts, definitions, and details, joined by linking words.

note.mistake: Children call every true sentence a fact, or call a sentence a definition because it has a hard word. When they write, many list facts and never tell what a hard word means.
note.words: Children need: headings (Introduce a topic and group the facts). Model first: read a short paragraph aloud and label one fact, one definition, and one detail. Say: "Each part starts with a fact. A definition tells what a word means. A detail tells more about the fact in its part." Day 1, Fact, Definition, or Detail?: children check the job of each sentence of a paragraph about a model topic, in parts: two parts in a table on Level 1, defined words in bold; three parts in a table on Level 2; numbered running text on Level 3. Then they add a definition and a detail to a fact. Day 2, Develop Your Topic: children write each part from its notes, define the word in one part, use linking words, and write a concluding sentence. Day 2 prints three definition frames (four on Level 3); Day 1 practices one definition and one detail. Level 1 prints the headings and starts every sentence; Level 2 starts each part;
note.watch: Ask, "Does this sentence tell what a word means? Does it tell more about the fact of its part?" A detail can be a number, an example, or what something looks like. On Day 2 the key is a sample; accept any sentence that tells what the word means, with or without a frame.

3:short-research-report.title: A short research report
3:short-research-report.objective: Children answer a research question from two short sources: notes by category, then a short report with headings, a diagram, and sources.

note.mistake: Children take all their notes from one source, or copy sentences. In the report they list notes or leave out the concluding sentence or the sources.
note.words: Children need the introduction, headings, and definitions of the last three lessons. Say: "A research report answers a question with facts from two sources." Read the question and both texts aloud. Model first on another topic: one short note with its source letter. Before Day 2, model turning one note from A and one from B into two sentences under a heading, and copying a source title. Day 1, Notes from Two Sources: children note facts from A and B in the row of each category. Level 1 prints the categories; on Level 2 children name them; on Level 3 they also write the question. Days 2 and 3, Write a Research Report (same copy, same topic as Day 1): children write an introduction, three parts with headings, a concluding sentence, and the source titles, and draw a diagram with a caption. Levels 1 and 2 print one note from each source in each part; Level 3 uses the child's own notes.
note.watch: Check each child's research question before they read: the sources must answer it. Each row needs a note from both sources; if both sources give a fact, either letter is right. If you can, add a third source: a class library book on the topic; children list it as C. The key is a sample.

2:plan-an-opinion.title: Plan an opinion: reasons and linking words
2:plan-an-opinion.objective: Children state an opinion about a topic and plan two or three reasons with linking words (because, and, also) and a closing sentence.

note.mistake: Children write a fact about themselves (I like pandas) instead of a view others can disagree with (Pandas are the best animals at the zoo), give a reason that does not tell why, or end with the opinion word for word.
note.words: Children need no page from an earlier lesson. Model first on a topic that is on no page: plan one piece about pandas on the board. Say: "An opinion tells what you think. A reason tells why. A closing sentence says the opinion again in new words, often with That is why." Day 1, Parts of an Opinion Piece: children write the letter of each mixed-up sentence of a short piece in the plan, then circle because, also, or and in gaps. On Level 3 one reason has no opener, and one sentence does not belong. Day 2, Plan Your Opinion Piece: children circle question A or B and plan: Level 1 frames, Level 2 starters (I think, because, also, That is why), Level 3 open rows, three reasons, and a word bank. Grey examples are on another topic: Level 1 fills the frames for another question; Levels 2 and 3 give notes on an animal or something in nature.
note.watch: Read each gap aloud with both words: because joins two sentences; in these gaps, also comes right before a doing word (They also hide nuts), and joins two words (black and white). The key's plan is a sample; accept any opinion whose reasons tell why.

2:draft-an-opinion.title: Draft an opinion piece
2:draft-an-opinion.objective: Children draft an opinion piece from their plan, with an opinion sentence that names the topic (the introduction at Grade 2), reasons joined by linking words, and a closing sentence (the standard's concluding statement).

note.mistake: Children copy their notes without making sentences, join every reason with and into one long sentence, or end with a new idea instead of their opinion again.
note.words: Children need their plan from Plan Your Opinion Piece: the draft of a copy number offers the two questions of the plan of that number; a child without a plan circles one. Model first on a topic that is on no page: "because they eat bamboo all day" becomes "One reason is that they eat bamboo all day." Day 1, Write Your Opinion Piece: rows under Opinion, Reasons, and Closing sentence. Level 1 frames (the second reason: It is also great because ___.), Level 2 starters, Level 3 open rows, three reasons, and a word bank. Day 2: reread with the checklist and add the spare-row sentence (Levels 1 and 2) or the third reason (Level 3). Day 3, Revise Your Opinion Piece: children circle what fits each gap of a short piece: the closing sentence (Level 1), a reason (Level 2), or both (Level 3); a partner listens and both check the parts; then the child writes one more reason (Level 1) or a reason or a closing sentence (Levels 2 and 3) and adds it with a caret (^).
note.watch: The opinion copied after That is why is never the closing sentence. The keys are samples; accept any reason that tells why.

2:friendly-letter.title: A friendly letter
2:friendly-letter.objective: Children write a friendly letter with a date, a greeting, a body, a closing, and a signature, and use commas after the greeting and the closing.

note.mistake: Children leave out the commas, put the comma after Dear (Dear, Sam), or write the closing and the signature on one line. Some forget the date.
note.words: Model first: write a short letter on the board and name the five parts: date (some programs call it the heading), greeting, body, closing, signature. Say: "A comma goes right after the greeting and right after the closing: Dear Sam, ... Your friend," Day 1, Parts of a Friendly Letter: children write the name of each part on the line beside it, using the word bank. Level 1 tells them where the two commas go; on Level 2 they find the two missing commas; on Level 3 one comma is in the wrong place, so they cross it out and add the two that belong. Levels 2 and 3 say that the date keeps its comma. Levels 1 and 2 end with greetings and closings to circle; Level 3 asks for a greeting and a closing to another reader. Day 2, Write a Friendly Letter: children need the five parts from day 1. They circle who they will write to and write about the topic on the page. Level 1 gives a frame on the first three rows of the body, Level 2 starters, Level 3 open rows. Grey examples come from a letter of another kind (Level 1: none under Body; Level 3: none).
note.watch: The bodies hold no other comma. The day-2 topic is never the kind of the day-1 letter of the same copy. The keys are samples.

2:capitals-special-names.title: Capitals for holidays, places, and brand names
2:capitals-special-names.objective: Children capitalize holidays, product names, and geographic names in sentences: each big word of a holiday or a place, and the brand of a product.

note.mistake: Children capitalize every noun (River, Park), or only the first word of a name (Hudson river), or the thing after a brand (Pemmo Paper). Some capitalize seasons (Winter) because holidays have capitals.
note.words: Model first: write "the river" and "Hudson River" on the board. Say: "In the name of a holiday or a place, each big word starts with a capital letter: Groundhog Day, Hudson River. Small words such as of stay small: Statue of Liberty. In a product name, only the brand gets a capital, not the thing: Pemmo paper." The product names on the pages are made up, so no real brand is on them. Day 1, Find the Capital Letters: children circle each word that is missing its capital letter in six sentences, then sort words in a table. Level 1 has holidays only; Level 2 holidays and places with pairs (a lake and the name of a lake), each word written again; Level 3 sorts names: holiday, place, or product name. Day 2, Write the Capital Letters: children need the rules from day 1; they write each sentence again with its capitals. Level 3 ends with a sentence about their own town, city, or state.
note.watch: Seasons and words such as holiday, river, and street stay small unless they are part of a name. No sentence starts with a name: the first word already has its capital, so every capital to add belongs to a name.

3:chapters-scenes-stanzas.title: Chapters, scenes, and stanzas
3:chapters-scenes-stanzas.objective: Children refer to the parts of stories, plays, and poems (chapter, scene, stanza) and describe how each part builds on the one before.

note.mistake: Children call every part a chapter, or count the lines of a poem as stanzas. Asked how a part builds, they retell it instead of naming what it needs from the part before.
note.words: Say: "A long story is divided into chapters. A play is divided into scenes. A poem is divided into stanzas: groups of lines with a space between them." Model with a second copy of the page (every copy has other texts), not the copy the children get. Before Scenes and Stanzas, model with the play of that copy: point to the cast list, a scene heading, and a stage direction, then answer its build question aloud with "In Scene 2, ___ because in Scene 1, ___." Level 1 circles; Level 2 writes on that frame and on "In Stanza 3, ___."; Level 3 writes what Stanza 3 adds and a Scene 3. Before Chapters: How Parts Build (scene and stanza from day 1), model one answer of a second copy with "In Chapter 2, ___ because in Chapter 1, ___." Level 1 circles, Level 2 writes on the frames, Level 3 fills a chart of what happens in each chapter, circles one chapter, and writes how one chapter builds on the one before.
note.watch: The stanzas are not numbered: children count them from left to right. The chapter titles do not give the answers: send children back into the chapter.

3:point-of-view.title: Whose point of view?
3:point-of-view.objective: Children tell their own point of view apart from that of the narrator or a character, and explain where they agree or disagree.

note.mistake: Children think the narrator is always the main character, or they write their own opinion when asked what a character thinks.
note.words: Say: "A point of view is what someone thinks about something. The narrator tells the story. A narrator who says I and my is a character in the story. Words in quotation marks are what a character says." Model with a second copy of the page (every copy has other texts), not the copy the children get. Before Who Is Telling the Story?, model with the story of a second copy: look for I or my outside the quotation marks, then answer its "What do YOU think?" aloud with "I think ___ because ___." Level 1 circles the teller and who thinks each sentence; Level 2 also circles how they know; Level 3 writes the teller and how they know. Before Their View and My View (the words narrator and quotation marks from day 1), model on a second copy what a character thinks and what you think. Level 1 circles the view and its proof and writes on the frame; Level 2 fills a chart and copies a proof; Level 3 also retells a paragraph with I and my.
note.watch: In a story told by an outside narrator, characters can still say I inside quotation marks. Each "What I think" box prints its question.

3:literal-nonliteral.title: Literal and nonliteral language
3:literal-nonliteral.objective: Children tell literal from nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context (take steps, a piece of cake, raining cats and dogs).

note.mistake: Children read a saying word by word (a piece of cake means cake), or they call every saying nonliteral, even in a sentence that uses its words in their plain meaning (Our puppy sleeps in the doghouse).
note.words: Say: "Literal words mean just what they say. Nonliteral words mean something else. The rest of the sentence tells you which." Before the page, model with a saying that is on no copy of the page: "Our puppy sleeps in the doghouse." (literal) and "I'm in the doghouse for being late." (nonliteral: in trouble), and read each sentence again with the meaning in place of the bold words. Day 1, Literal or Nonliteral?: every sentence has one bold phrase, and every page has at least two literal and two nonliteral sentences. Level 1: six sentences; children circle literal or nonliteral, then circle what the words mean here: what the words say, what the saying means, or a meaning that fits neither. Level 2: eight sentences; children write L or N in the box and write the meaning. Level 3: six sentences, then two sentences of their own with sayings from a box, each printed with its meaning. Day 2, on screen, Gabby's Funny Sayings — What Does It Really Mean? (Grade 3): every round there is nonliteral, so day 2 practices meanings: children read a saying in a sentence and tap what it really means (eight sayings, such as raining cats and dogs, hit the hay, and let the cat out of the bag).
note.watch: Some sayings have no literal sentence on the page (raining cats and dogs, under the weather): they are always nonliteral. The key's written meanings and sentences are samples.

3:two-books-one-author.title: Two books by one author
3:two-books-one-author.objective: Children compare and contrast the themes, settings, and plots of two stories by the same author about the same or similar characters.

note.mistake: Children compare only the characters, who are the same in both stories, or they retell one story instead of telling what is alike and what is different.
note.words: Say: "These two stories have one author and the same characters. We compare the setting (where and when), the problem, how it is solved, and the lesson." Model with a second copy of the page (every copy has other texts), not the copy the children get. Before Two Stories by One Author, model one sentence of a second copy: find it in each story before you circle Both. Level 1: seven sentences to circle Story 1, Story 2, or Both; Level 2: eight, and one sentence on "In both stories, ___."; Level 3: five, then "In both stories, ___." and "In Story 1, ___, but in Story 2, ___." Before Compare Two Stories (the words setting, problem, and lesson; any pair works, it need not be the day-1 pair), model one row of the chart of a second copy aloud. Level 1: gray examples, a strip letter in each box, two strips crossed out; Level 2: the examples and six boxes to write; Level 3: all eight boxes.
note.watch: A sentence is Both only if each story says it. The authors and stories were written for these pages. The key's chart notes and sentences are samples.

3:two-texts-one-topic.title: Two texts on one topic
3:two-texts-one-topic.objective: Children compare and contrast the most important points and key details in two information texts on the same topic.

note.mistake: Children mark a fact Both because it fits the topic, without finding it in each text, or they name a detail as the most important point.
note.words: Say: "The most important point is what the whole text is mostly about. Key details tell more about it." Model with a second copy of the page (every copy has other texts), not the copy the children get. Before Two Texts on One Topic, model one fact of a second copy: underline it in each text where you find it. Level 1 writes the letters of eight facts in the two-circle diagram; Levels 2 and 3 have ten, two of them in neither text, to cross out; Level 3 also writes how the texts are different. Before Compare Two Texts (underlining a fact in each text, as on day 1), model with one text of a second copy how a detail tells about one part and the point covers it all. Level 1 circles each text's point among its own details and the detail both texts give; Level 2 fills a chart and writes something both tell; Level 3 writes how the texts are alike and how they are different.
note.watch: Have children underline each fact where they find it. A fact in neither text is true, but it is not in these texts. A title can hint at the point; check the point against the whole text.

1:true-story-plan-and-draft.title: Write a true story: plan and draft
1:true-story-plan-and-draft.objective: Children plan a true story in three parts (first, next, last) and an ending, then draft it in sentences that start with time words and close with how it ended.

note.mistake: Children tell one event, or list events with no order and no ending. Some start every sentence with And then, or stop after Last.
note.words: Model first: tell a short true story of your own (feeding the class fish) and sketch it in three boxes. Say: "A true story tells what happened first, next, and last, and how it ended." Day 1, Plan a True Story: read the story with the class; children circle the time words (on Levels 2 and 3 some stories say Then or After that for Next) and number three sentences from it 1, 2, 3. Levels 2 and 3 also underline the ending; on Level 3 one sentence is not in the story and gets an X. Each child circles one of two ideas or My own idea, draws in the boxes (three on Level 1, four on Levels 2 and 3), and writes a few words beside each; Level 1 gives feeling words for the end. Days 2 and 3, Write a True Story: children write from their plan. Level 1 starts the sentences with First, I / Next, I / Last, I / I felt; Level 2 with First, / Next, / Last, / At the end,; Level 3 has open rows and a word bank. Read the model (another day) first; children check the boxes at the end.
note.watch: Children retell in order from Kindergarten. Keep each plan for days 2 and 3. The day 1 story is never one of the ideas. Accept Then or After that for Next, and a feeling or what happened at the end as the ending.

1:opinion-and-reason.title: My opinion and a reason
1:opinion-and-reason.objective: Children tell an opinion from a reason, match each opinion with the reason that supports it, and write a piece: the topic, an opinion with because and a reason, and an ending.

note.mistake: Children give a reason that fits any opinion (it is fun), or leave out because. Some write I like tag. Help them say what they think: I think tag is the best game.
note.words: Model first: write I think pancakes are the best breakfast because they are warm and sweet. Circle because and underline the reason. Say: "An opinion tells what you think. A reason tells why you think so." Day 1, Opinion or Reason?: on Levels 1 and 2 read the sort sentences aloud once; children check opinion or reason for each, draw a line from each opinion to its reason, and circle because (Levels 2 and 3 also underline the reason). Read the opinions and the reasons aloud once; then children test each reason by saying the opinion, because, and the reason. On Level 3 one reason fits no opinion: children cross it out. Day 2, Write My Opinion: each child circles a question, draws the answer, and writes the topic, the opinion with because, and an ending. Level 1 gives frames, Level 2 starters, Level 3 open rows and a word bank. On Levels 1 and 2 the model beside the drawing answers another question. Post the titles of the books the class read so children can spell them.
note.watch: From the lesson before: sentences with an end mark. The ending says the opinion again in new words. Accept any reason that tells why.

1:all-about-a-topic.title: All about a topic: facts and a closing
1:all-about-a-topic.objective: Children name a topic, tell sentences about the topic from sentences that are not about it, choose a closing sentence, and write an All About page: the topic, three facts, and a closing.

note.mistake: Children add a sentence about something else (a pond on a page about ducks), or end with one more fact instead of a closing. Some write an opinion, such as Ducks are cute, as a fact.
note.words: Model first: say three facts about pumpkins (Pumpkins grow on vines. Pumpkins have seeds. Pumpkins can be orange.) and close: Now you know about pumpkins! Say: "A fact tells something true about the topic. A closing sentence ends the piece." Day 1, Facts and a Closing: read the fact file together; children write its topic, put a check under yes or no for each sentence (is it about the topic?), and circle the closing. On Level 3 one sentence is about a thing near the topic, such as a pond, and is not about it. Day 2, Write an All About Page: Level 1 uses the fact box and frames such as Cows eat; on Level 2 the fact box gives the notes without their verbs, and children choose can, have, are, eat, or live; on Level 3 children choose a topic they know, such as rain or my school, and write on open rows with one to spare. Each child draws the topic and writes two labels, then checks the boxes. On Levels 1 and 2 the model is about another topic.
note.watch: From the lessons before: capitals and end marks. Every fact on day 1 names its topic. On Level 3 accept any true fact; each one should name the topic.

1:revise-and-edit-checklist.title: Revise and edit with a checklist
1:revise-and-edit-checklist.objective: Children fix capitals and end marks in a short piece, add a detail a partner asked about, and check their own piece with a checklist and a partner.

note.mistake: Children fix only the first mistake they see, or add a detail that does not answer the question. Some copy the whole piece again instead of fixing it.
note.words: Model first: write we went on a walk, fix it aloud, then ask a child a question about your sentence and add the answer. Say: "Writers read their work again. They fix capitals and end marks, and they add details." Day 1, Edit and Add a Detail: the box says how many mistakes the story has (Level 1: two, a small letter at the start and a missing end mark; Level 2: three, with a small i; Level 3: four, with a name that starts with a small letter). Children fix them on the story, read the question the writer's partner asked about the starred sentence, and write it again with a detail. Day 2, Revise with a Checklist: each child needs a draft from this unit (the true story, the opinion, or the All About page). The partner asks one question; the child circles it (or writes it after Other), adds the detail to the draft with a caret (^), and writes it on the page. Then the child checks the draft in the Me boxes and the partner checks it too; Level 3 also writes what the partner liked.
note.watch: The day 1 story has no other mistake; where a missing end mark could also be !, the key says so. Accept any detail that answers the question. The partner asks one question, not a list.

2:plan-informative-piece.title: Plan an informative piece
2:plan-informative-piece.objective: Children name the parts of an informative piece and plan one: a topic sentence, facts under headings, a definition, a closing sentence.

note.mistake: Children start with one fact, not a sentence about the whole topic, leave an opinion or a sentence about something else among the facts, or sort a fact by one shared word.
note.words: Children need: Animal fact file. Model first on sloths, a topic on no page: group five facts under two headings, then write a topic sentence and a closing sentence. Say: "An informative piece tells only facts, and every sentence is about its topic. A closing sentence tells about the topic again at the end, in new words." Day 1: children underline the topic sentence of a short piece and box its closing sentence; Levels 2 and 3 also circle the definition. Then they sort facts about another topic under two headings and cross out what does not belong: a sentence about something else (Level 1), an opinion (Level 2), or both (Level 3). Day 2: a box gives five facts and a definition. Children plan a topic sentence, three facts, a definition, and a closing sentence: Level 1 with frames, Level 2 with starters and two of three headings to choose. Level 3 in notes: children name two headings and use a word bank.
note.watch: Ask: does it tell about the whole topic, or one part? People can disagree with an opinion, so an informative piece leaves it out. The key's plan is a sample; accept any facts from the box under a heading they fit.

2:draft-facts-closing.title: Draft with facts and a closing
2:draft-facts-closing.objective: Children draft an informative piece from their plan, with a topic sentence, facts joined by linking words, a definition, and a closing sentence.

note.mistake: Children end with a new fact or the topic sentence again, or put another where also belongs (They another swim).
note.words: Children need: their plan from the lesson before. Model first on moose, a topic on no page: a topic sentence, two facts joined with also, a definition (a bull is a grown male moose), and a closing sentence. Say: "A closing sentence tells about the topic again in new words. It gives no new fact." Day 1: children circle the closing sentence that fits a short piece; wrong choices add a new fact (on Levels 2 and 3 one starts with Now you know), give an opinion about something else (Levels 1 and 3), or copy the topic sentence (Levels 2 and 3). They finish a definition (Level 1), write the word too (Level 2) or all of it (Level 3), and circle also, another, or and for each blank. Day 2: children write from their plan or the six sentences at the top. Level 1 has frames, Level 2 starters and an open row for a linking word, Level 3 open lines and a word bank.
note.watch: Another comes before one thing (another kind), also before a doing word (They also swim), and the word and joins two things or actions (seeds and bugs). At the start of a sentence, Also takes a comma: Also, moose eat water plants. On these pages a closing sentence gives no new fact; a 'wow fact' is a fact, not a closing sentence.

2:research-class-report.title: Research with two books: a class report
2:research-class-report.objective: Children take notes from two short books on one topic, tell which book each fact came from, and write one part of a class report.

note.mistake: Children copy whole sentences, drop some or many so the note says more than the book, or mark one book when both tell a fact.
note.words: Children need: Draft with facts and a closing. Model on garbage trucks, a topic on no page. Book 1: "A garbage truck picks up trash from homes." Note: trash from homes. Book 2: "Most garbage trucks crush the trash they pick up." Note: most crush the trash. Say: "A note is a few words. It keeps the fact true, and we write which book it came from." Day 1: read both books aloud together first; children fill the table with a partner, then take notes: Level 1 copies a few words, Level 2 uses own words, Level 3 also writes 1, 2, or B. Day 2: give each child the same copy number on both days and hand back the day-1 page. Levels 1 and 2 print all three headings with their notes; children circle the one you give them. Give each table one heading so that every heading has writers. Level 3 children choose a heading and use their notes. They write a heading and three sentences and draw a labeled picture. Cut out the parts on the dashed line; sort them by heading behind a cover with the question and both titles. Write the report's topic sentence and closing sentence together on the cover.
note.watch: Ask: which book told you that? If both tell it, Both is right. Accept any short note that keeps the fact true.

2:true-story-plan-draft.title: Plan and draft a true story
2:true-story-plan-draft.objective: Children plan a true story of one small moment and draft it in order with time words, one thing they thought or felt, and an ending.

note.mistake: Children tell a whole day (school, then lunch, then home) instead of one small moment, or stop after the last event with no ending.
note.words: Model first: tell the class a true story about finding a ladybug on the slide (you felt happy), then plan it aloud in the four boxes. Day 1: before the page, circle its time words and underline how you felt on the board. Day 3: write its beginning and first event on the board from your plan. Children need the time words from the retelling lesson. Say: "A true story tells what happened to me, in order." Day 1, Parts of a True Story: children circle the 3 time words, underline the sentence that tells a feeling or a thought, number three events, and circle the ending (Level 3 writes one). Day 2, Plan Your True Story: children circle an idea or write their own and make notes; Level 1 has frames, Level 2 starters, Level 3 a word bank. Day 3, Draft Your True Story: children write from their plan under Beginning, Middle, and Ending; Level 3 also adds one detail.
note.watch: If a story tells what usually happens ('We play tag every day'), ask: "What did you see? What did you think?" An ending wraps up the moment; it does not start something new.

2:revise-edit-story.title: Revise and edit a story with a checklist
2:revise-edit-story.objective: Children reread their story draft with a partner, add a detail, and fix capital letters and end marks with a checklist.

note.mistake: Children copy the story without changing anything, or change something that was right, such as a comma after a time word.
note.words: Model first: read aloud a short draft of your own about your walk to school; let the class ask one question and add the answer as a detail; then fix one capital letter and one end mark. Children need the story they drafted in the last lesson. Say: "Writers reread, add details, and fix mistakes." Day 1, Edit a Story, practices on a second grader's story: the box counts the mistakes; children write each capital above its small letter and add the end marks; Level 2 also numbers the sentences, Level 3 reads one paragraph and crosses out the sentence that does not belong; then they write the two sentences with two mistakes again. Day 2, Revise with a Partner, uses this on their own draft: they read it to a partner, look at it together, check it as Me and Partner (3, 5, or 6 checks by level), and write the partner's question, the detail they added, and a sentence they fixed or checked; Level 3 starts with what the partner liked. Children add the detail to their draft with a caret (^) and copy it here.
note.watch: The partner asks; the writer decides. In the story to edit, only the counted mistakes are wrong. A missing end mark takes a period; an exclamation mark is right too where the sentence could be said with strong feeling.

2:story-beginning-ending.title: How a story begins and ends
2:story-beginning-ending.objective: Children describe how the beginning of a story introduces the characters, the setting, and the problem, and how the ending solves the problem.

note.mistake: Children name something a character tries in the middle as the way the problem is solved, or say a character who first comes in later was met in the beginning.
note.words: Model first with a story of your own: "Sam and his dad sat on the sand. The wind took Sam's umbrella. They ran after it. At last, a lifeguard caught it." Say: "The beginning tells who, where, and the problem. The middle tells what the characters try. The ending tells how the problem is solved." Children need to know from Grade 1 that a story has characters, a setting, and events. Day 1, How a Story Begins and Ends: children read a story in three labeled parts, circle the problem and how it is solved, and write B, M, or E beside sentences about the story. Level 2 adds a sentence about whom we first meet; Level 3 offers a smaller trouble of the middle as a wrong problem and one sentence the story does not tell (X). Day 2, Write How a Story Begins and Ends: Level 1 finishes frames, Level 2 starters; on Level 3 children answer in their own words and write a new ending, or a beginning when the story starts in the middle. Day 2 uses a new story; children need the three parts from day 1.
note.watch: Ask: "Is the problem solved yet?" A sentence from the middle tells a try that does not work. The answers on the keys are samples, and each key says what else is right.

2:character-voices.title: Different voices for different characters
2:character-voices.objective: Children notice that characters see the same thing in different ways and read each character's words in a voice that fits that character.

note.mistake: Children give a line to the character named last before it instead of the one named with said, or read every part in the same voice.
note.words: Model first on the board: Grandpa Walt said, "Pajamas on, please." "Five more minutes!" begged Ziggy. Then: Theo shivered. "Brr, it is cold in here!" Who is talking? Theo, because he does something right before the words. Read Grandpa Walt in a calm voice and Ziggy in a pleading voice. Say: "Quotation marks show a character's words. The name and 'said' tell who is talking." From the lesson before, children need the characters of a story. Day 1, Who Is Talking: children write the letter of the speaker of each numbered line, from the list under the story; a box on the page shows how (Level 1 four lines named after the words, Level 2 six, some named before the words, Level 3 eight, some named only in an action sentence beside the words). Then they write who thinks each view, or X for nobody. Day 2, Reader's Theater: children circle a voice word for each character. Then groups of four read the play: give each child a part (a narrator and three characters), read it twice, and switch parts. Level 3 also writes one more line for the first character.
note.watch: Listen for voices that match the words children circled. Words in ( ) tell how to read a line and are not read aloud.

2:two-versions-of-a-tale.title: Two versions of one tale
2:two-versions-of-a-tale.objective: Children compare and contrast two versions of the same story, such as two tellings of a folktale in different places or with different characters.

note.mistake: Children mark a fact Both because it is true of the tale they know, without finding it in each version on the page.
note.words: Model first with two Cinderella stories the class knows: one with a glass slipper and one with a golden shoe. Say: "Two versions tell the same tale. Some parts are the same, and some are different. Check each version before you say Both." From the lesson before, children need the characters, setting, problem, and ending of a story; the chart uses these parts. The versions were written for these pages: each tells a well-known tale with new animals or in a new place. Day 1, Sort the Facts: children read both versions and circle 1, 2, or Both for six or seven facts about the characters, setting, problem, and ending; Level 3 adds Neither. Day 2, Compare Them: On day 2, give each child the same copy number as on day 1 and hand back the day-1 page; the chart sums up the two versions they read. Children write how the versions are alike and different and which one they like better and why (Level 1 frames and a version to circle, Level 2 starters, Level 3 their own words).
note.watch: Ask for the sentence in each version that tells a fact. Any reason from the tale is right for the version a child likes better.

2:build-on-others-talk.title: Book club talk: build on what others say
2:build-on-others-talk.objective: Children build on what others say in a book talk by linking their comments to what others said.

note.mistake: Children take a turn but change the subject: they tell something about themselves instead of linking to an idea someone said.
note.words: Before day 2, read one picture book aloud to the class; the card is about that book. Model first in a fishbowl with two children and one idea that is on no page: "I think the lighthouse keeper was brave." Show a reply that builds on it and one that does not. Say: "To build on what someone said, start with their idea: I agree with ___ because, I want to add that, or I see it another way." From the lessons before, children need to tell what characters do and why. Day 1, Build on What Others Say: children read a tiny story and circle the reply that builds on each child's comment (Level 1 two replies, Levels 2 and 3 three; Level 3 also offers a reply about the story that ignores the idea, and children write a reply). Day 2, Book Club Talk Card: before the talk children write one thing to say about the book and one question; groups of four talk, and a name stick picks the first speaker; after the talk children write whose idea they built on, that idea, and what they said, then check the list. The card works with any book: read it aloud, give each child a card, and talk in groups of four.
note.watch: Listen for comments that link to what others said and for reasons from the book.

K:opinion-favorite-why.title: My favorite and why: an opinion
K:opinion-favorite-why.objective: Children tell what they like best and why: they find the opinion and the reason in short pieces, then draw and write their own.

note.mistake: Children name a favorite and give no reason, or give a reason that does not tell why they like it (blue because it is a color).
note.words: Model first on chart paper. Say: "My favorite time of day is night because it is quiet." Point to the part that tells what you like and the part that tells why. Read every instruction, sentence, and word bank aloud, pointing to each. A class vote with Class Graph (each child taps an answer) helps before day 2. Day 1, What I Like Best and Why: children circle what they like best in each row (any choice is right). Read each piece; children circle the sentence that tells what the writer likes best and draw a line under the sentence that tells why. On Level 3 the first sentence tells the topic and gets no mark. Day 2, My Favorite and Why: children circle one of three topics or my own, draw, and write. Level 1 prints My favorite, is, and because it is, with a word bank of reason words (a child may use his or her own word); Level 2 prints My favorite and because; Level 3 starts with I and has a word bank. A grey model on another topic shows the shape.
note.watch: Accept sounded-out spelling: fn for fun is right. A child who cannot yet write a word may tell it, and you write it. Check that the reason fits its thing: blue because it is cool is a reason.

K:fact-draw-label-write.title: Teach a fact: draw, label, and write
K:fact-draw-label-write.objective: Children name a topic, draw and label it, and write one or two facts about it.

note.mistake: Children write a sentence about something else (A cow says moo. on a cat page), or label a part with the name of the whole animal.
note.words: Model first: draw a snail and label its shell and feelers. Say: "A snail can crawl. A snail has a shell." Read every instruction, sentence, and word bank aloud, pointing to each; read each sentence twice. Day 1, Facts and Labels: children put a check mark in the box of each sentence about the pictured animal, thing, or plant and an X in the box of the one about something else. Then they label two parts: Level 1 cuts out two cards and glues each in the box its line comes from; Levels 2 and 3 write the words of the word bank on the lines (on Level 3 one word names no part). Extra practice for day 1: the screen activity The Wobble Museum — Stick to the Topic (find the sentence about something else). Day 2, I Can Teach You a Fact: children circle one of three animals or my own, draw it, write two labels beside the box with a line to each part, and finish A ___ can ___ and A ___ has ___ (Level 1 with a word bank, Level 2 sounded out; Level 3 starts with A and has a word bank).
note.watch: Accept sounded-out spelling: wng for wing is right. A child who cannot yet write a word may tell it, and you write it. If an animal starts with a, e, i, o, or u, help the child write An. Ask, "How do you know?" A fact is something true that you saw or learned.

K:small-moment-draw-write.title: What happened to me: a small moment
K:small-moment-draw-write.objective: Children tell one small moment in the order it happened, draw and write it, and tell how they felt.

note.mistake: Children tell a whole day (I got up. I ate. I went to school.) instead of one small moment, or leave out how they felt.
note.words: Model first: draw three boxes. Say: "I found a feather. I showed my teacher. I put it on the science table. I felt proud." Read every instruction and word aloud, pointing to each. Day 1, Put a Small Moment in Order: the sentences are printed out of order. Read the sentences as they are printed, pointing to each; read them again. Ask, "What happened first?" Children write 1 in that box, then 2 and 3 (Level 3: 1 to 4). Then they circle the face that shows how the writer felt (the last sentence shows it) and draw what happened last. Day 2, My Small Moment: children circle one of two moments or my own and draw it in three boxes: first, next, last. Level 1 writes I ___ for the last box and I felt ___; Levels 2 and 3 write I ___ beside each small box; on Level 3 the faces have no words and a word bank stands beside First.
