note.watch: Accept sounded-out spelling. A child who cannot yet write a word may tell it, and you write it. Let a child say each sentence aloud before writing it; ask, "What happened next?" Mad means angry.

K:authors-chair-add-detail.title: Author's chair: a friend asks, I add
K:authors-chair-add-detail.objective: Children read their writing to the class, answer a classmate's question, and add one detail to the picture or the words.

note.mistake: Friends give praise (I like it.) instead of a question, or the author answers out loud but adds nothing to the page.
note.words: Model first with your own piece: read "I made a mask." A child asks, "What animal is it?" Say: "It is a fox mask." and add the detail with a colored pencil. Read every instruction, question, and sentence aloud, pointing to each. Day 1, A Friend Asks, I Add: read each piece, its question, and the sentences; children circle the sentence that answers the question (on Level 3 one choice only says the piece again). Day 2, Author's Chair: each author gets this page; staple it to the piece he or she read. Three children a day sit in the author's chair and read a piece they wrote in this unit. Pull a name with Name Sticks; that child asks one question. On Level 1 the friend asks with one of the four starters on the page, and the author circles it; on Levels 2 and 3 you or the friend write the question on the row. The author draws the new detail in the box and writes it (Level 1 one word, Level 2 one row, Level 3 a sentence), then checks I shared, I listened, and I added a detail.
note.watch: Accept sounded-out spelling. A child who cannot yet write a word may tell it, and you write it. Children need a finished piece from this unit. Teach questions that ask for a detail: Who? What? Where? When? A yes-or-no question gets no detail.

1:first-middle-last-sound.title: First, middle, or last sound?
1:first-middle-last-sound.objective: Children isolate and say the first, middle, and last sound of a spoken one-syllable word and mark where they hear a given sound.

note.mistake: Children say a letter name instead of the sound, or hear the two sounds at the start of a word like step as one.
note.words: Children can blend and segment three-sound words. Model with mop and step, which are on no page. Say: “Mop: /m/ /ŏ/ /p/. /m/ is first, /ŏ/ is in the middle, /p/ is last.” Each box is one sound: mop has three boxes, step has four. Day 1, G1-624: read the teacher lines at the foot of the answer key: the picture word, then the sound. Level 1: the first or last sound; children color its box. Level 2: first, middle, or last; the middle sound is the vowel of a word with three sounds. Level 3: children write the letter in its box. Day 2, G1-625: read the picture words from the answer key first; children say the sounds of each picture, touching a box for each, and circle where the two words share a sound (level 1: first or last; level 2: any place). Level 3: rows of three pictures; children circle the two that share a sound, then its place.
note.watch: In a word with four sounds (step) only the first and last sounds are asked, never the first of dr or tr (many children hear /j/ or /ch/). Some children say the vowel of pen, dog, bag, or leg another way, so these are never asked for their middle sound. If a child colors the wrong box, say the word slowly and touch one box a sound.

K:onset-rime-blend.title: Blend the first sound and the rest
K:onset-rime-blend.objective: Children blend a spoken first sound and the rest of a one-syllable word (/m/ … /ŏp/) into the word and find its picture, and they split a word into its first sound and the rest.

note.mistake: Children name a picture as soon as they hear the first sound, without the rest. Some add a vowel to a first sound (/buh/ for /b/).
note.words: Children should already hear the first sound of a word and hear rhymes. Model with words that are on no page (mop, man, sit, top). Say: “Listen: /m/ … /ŏp/. I put the parts together: mop. Your turn: /s/ … /ĭt/.” Day 1, K-681: read the teacher lines at the foot of the answer key, row by row: the first sound, a short wait, then the rest; never the whole word. Level 1: the first sound alone finds the word; still say the rest. Level 2: one first sound a row, so only the rest decides. Level 3: some pictures rhyme, some start alike: children need both parts. Day 2, K-682: name each picture for the class first. A child says a picture word in two parts, touching the small box (first sound) and the long box (the rest); a partner blends it. Level 1 words start with a sound you can stretch (/mmm/), level 2 with one you cannot (/b/). Level 3: circle the two that rhyme. On the screen: Blend Onset and Rime — Listen and Find the Word.
note.watch: On level 2 a child who hears only the first sound cannot choose: watch who waits for the rest. Goat and coat differ only in /g/ and /k/: say them clearly. The key writes a short vowel with a curve (/ŏp/), a long one with a bar (/ōp/).

K:two-meanings.title: Words with two meanings
K:two-meanings.objective: Children find the two meanings of a familiar word (a bat that flies, a bat for baseball) and choose the meaning that fits a sentence.

note.mistake: Children pick the meaning they know best without listening to the sentence, or think one of the two pictures has the wrong name.
note.words: Children know the everyday meaning of each word. Model with duck, which is on no page. Say: “A duck is a bird. When a ball flies at you, you duck: you bend down fast. One word, two meanings.” Day 1, K-683: read the word at the start of each row, then its sentence two times from the teacher lines at the foot of the answer key; children circle the picture of what the word means in that sentence. Level 1: two pictures a row. Level 2: one more picture of something else. Level 3: you read two sentences a word; children circle the picture for the first and draw a line under the picture for the second. Sometimes both sentences use the same meaning: then both marks go under one picture. Day 2, K-684: read each word; children draw a line from its picture to the other picture that the same word names (levels 2 and 3: one picture has no partner). Level 3: children draw the familiar meaning of two words and say a sentence with each.
note.watch: Ask, “Which words in the sentence tell you?” A child who names them (bend down fast, for duck) is listening. On level 3 the third picture is another word's meaning: only the sentence rules it out. Accept any true drawing; the key says what counts.

K:compare-two-stories.title: Two stories, two adventures
K:compare-two-stories.objective: Children compare what happens to the characters of two stories and tell one thing that is the same and one that is different.

note.mistake: Children sort a card by what could happen instead of what the story said, or put a card in Both because it is true of one story.
note.words: Children should already retell a story: who, where, what happened. Model with two tiny stories of your own: a cat loses a sock at school, a dog loses a sock at the park. Say: “Both lost a sock: that card goes in the middle, Both. Only the cat was at school: Story 1.” Day 1, K-685: read both stories two times, then each card: “Which story told us this? Or both?” Cut the cards before you sort, or sort first and glue last. Level 1: four cards; levels 2 and 3: five. Level 3: each child tells a partner one more thing that is the same. Day 2, K-686: choose a copy with another pair of stories. Name the faces first: happy, sad, tired, surprised, scared, angry. Children draw one thing that is the same and how the stories differ (Story 1 in box 1), then circle how each animal felt at the end. Level 3: children write a word for each drawing. Then use the same chart with two books your class knows. On the screen: Willow's Story Corner — Two Tales, Alike or Different? (Kindergarten).
note.watch: Every card is stated in its story: when a child disagrees, read the sentence back. A card goes in Story 1 only when Story 2 says something else. A sad face stands where the animal was sad before the end: the row asks about the end.
